This is one of the three headline benefits of running a hypervisor.
why_wrong: Better Utilisation is about using a server's full capacity instead of wasting it; it says nothing about what happens when a VM crashes.
Fast Disaster Recovery is the company use-case of restoring a crashed VM from a snapshot in minutes; the scenario is about the other VMs surviving, not about restoring the crashed one.
One Machine, Many OSes is the benefit that Windows and Ubuntu can share one laptop at all; the point here is that the crash did not spread, which is isolation.

questions.q: Priya installs VirtualBox on her laptop, downloads an Ubuntu Server ISO and installs it inside a new VM. In virtualisation terms, what are the laptop and the Ubuntu Server running inside the VM called, respectively?
questions.explain: The physical machine that provides the real CPU, RAM and disk is the host. Each operating system running inside a VM on top of the hypervisor is a guest. The stack is always physical host, then hypervisor, then guest OSes, so the laptop is the host and Ubuntu Server is a guest.
why_wrong: This reverses the roles: the guest is the OS living inside the VM, not the physical laptop that provides the hardware.
The hypervisor is VirtualBox itself, the software layer between host and guests; neither the laptop nor Ubuntu Server is the hypervisor.
The laptop is indeed the host, but Ubuntu Server is a guest OS running inside a VM, not the hypervisor that runs it.

questions.q: Sana has a Windows laptop and wants to try Linux for her programming course, but she cannot afford to lose Windows or any of her files. Which kind of hypervisor should she use, and why?
options: A Type 1 bare-metal hypervisor such as VMware ESXi, because it is faster
A Type 2 hosted hypervisor such as Oracle VirtualBox or VMware Workstation, because it runs on top of Windows and lets Linux run as a VM without deleting or replacing Windows
A Type 1 hypervisor such as KVM, because a Linux hypervisor is needed to run Linux guests
No hypervisor is needed; she must erase Windows and install Linux in its place
questions.explain: A hosted (Type 2) hypervisor is installed on Windows like any other application, and Linux then runs inside a virtual machine on top of it. Windows stays exactly as it is, her files are untouched, and she can delete the Linux VM at any time with no risk to the real machine. This is precisely the personal-use case that VirtualBox and VMware Workstation are built for.
why_wrong: A bare-metal hypervisor runs directly on the hardware with no host OS, so installing ESXi would mean replacing Windows rather than keeping it; speed is not the concern here.
KVM is a Type 1 bare-metal hypervisor used in data centres, and a hypervisor of either type can run Linux guests; what Sana needs is one that runs on top of her existing Windows.
That is exactly what she wants to avoid; a hosted hypervisor gives her Linux as a VM while Windows stays intact.

questions.q: A cloud provider is building a new data centre and needs each server to run as many customer VMs as possible with the highest performance. The team is deciding which hypervisor to install on the bare servers. Which choice fits, and why?
options: Oracle VirtualBox, because it is the simplest to set up
Parallels Desktop, because it supports many guest OSes side by side
A Type 1 bare-metal hypervisor such as VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V or KVM, because it runs directly on the hardware with no host OS and is faster
A Type 2 hosted hypervisor, because a host OS underneath makes each server more reliable
questions.explain: Data centres run Type 1 hypervisors: they are installed straight onto the server hardware, need no operating system underneath, and are therefore faster than hosted products. That performance is what lets one powerful server carry many VMs efficiently, which is the model AWS, Azure and Google Cloud run at massive scale. VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V, Citrix Hypervisor (XenServer) and KVM are the bare-metal options.
why_wrong: VirtualBox is a hosted Type 2 product meant for personal use; simple setup does not make up for needing a host OS underneath it on every server.
Parallels Desktop is a hosted Type 2 hypervisor for personal use; every hypervisor supports many guests, so that is not a reason to pick it for a data centre.
A host OS underneath is an extra layer that slows a hosted hypervisor down; it is the reason Type 2 is used for personal virtualisation rather than in data centres.

questions.q: Aditya uses a MacBook for college and wants to run Windows for one course tool while keeping macOS as his everyday system. Of the hypervisors covered, which product fits, and what type is it?
options: VMware ESXi, a Type 1 bare-metal hypervisor
VMware Fusion, a Type 2 hosted hypervisor
VMware Fusion, a Type 1 bare-metal hypervisor
questions.explain: VMware Fusion is the hosted hypervisor listed for the Mac: it installs as an application on macOS and runs Windows inside a VM alongside it, so macOS stays the everyday system. Because it runs on top of an existing OS it is Type 2, the type built for personal virtualisation. Its bare-metal sibling ESXi would take over the whole machine instead of living inside macOS.
why_wrong: ESXi is a bare-metal hypervisor that runs directly on the hardware with no host OS, so it would replace macOS rather than run beside it; it belongs in a data centre.
Fusion is the right product, but it is hosted on top of macOS, which makes it Type 2, not bare-metal Type 1.
KVM is a Type 1 bare-metal hypervisor used in data centres, not a hosted Mac application, and the type given here is wrong as well.

questions.q: In a lab session, Karan reads that VMware makes ESXi, Workstation and Fusion, and concludes that all three must be the same type of hypervisor. Which statement is correct?
options: All three are Type 1, because VMware is a data-centre company
All three are Type 2, because they are all installed as software
ESXi is Type 1 (bare-metal); Workstation and Fusion are Type 2 (hosted)
ESXi and Workstation are Type 1; only Fusion is Type 2 because it runs on a Mac
questions.explain: The type is decided by what the hypervisor runs on, not by who makes it. VMware ESXi installs directly on server hardware with no host OS, so it is bare-metal Type 1 and belongs in data centres. VMware Workstation and VMware Fusion (the Mac version) both run as applications on top of an existing OS, so both are hosted Type 2 products for personal use.
why_wrong: ESXi is indeed a data-centre bare-metal product, but Workstation and Fusion are hosted applications that run on top of an existing OS, which makes them Type 2.
Every hypervisor is software; the distinction is whether it runs on bare hardware (ESXi) or as an app on an existing OS (Workstation, Fusion), so they are not all Type 2.
Workstation runs on top of an existing OS just as Fusion does; running on a Mac is not what makes Fusion Type 2, being hosted on an OS is, and Workstation shares that.

questions.q: Arjun found a 'free video converter' on a random forum and wants to try it inside his Ubuntu VM. He is worried it might be malware, and he wants to be able to put the VM back exactly as it is right now in a moment if the app causes trouble. What should he do before running it?
options: Stop the VM cleanly, then start it again before installing the app
Clone the VM so a second full copy exists on disk
Take a snapshot of the VM
Delete the VM and create a fresh one after the test
questions.explain: A snapshot saves the VM's exact current state so you can return to it later. If the converter breaks something, installs malware or crashes the system, Arjun simply restores the snapshot and the VM is back to the working state it had before, with his real laptop never touched. Snapshot first, experiment second is the habit to build before trusting any unknown software.
why_wrong: Stop and Start only shut the VM down and boot it again; they save no restore point, so there would be nothing to roll back to.
Clone makes an identical second copy of the whole VM; it does not give the original VM a saved state to return to, which is exactly what a snapshot does.
Delete permanently removes the VM and frees its resources; doing it afterwards throws away his whole setup instead of returning it to the state it had before the test.

questions.q: Meera has spent a week setting up a Linux VM with every compiler, library and tool her group project needs. Her teammate Dev wants an exactly identical VM on his own laptop so they work in the same environment. Which VM management action gives Meera what she needs to hand over?
questions.explain: Clone makes an identical copy of the whole VM, its virtual disk, settings and everything installed on it, as a separate machine. That copy can be given to Dev and run on his laptop while Meera keeps her original, so both have the same environment. Cloning is how you duplicate a VM; the other actions only change the state of the one VM you already have.
why_wrong: A snapshot saves the exact state of the same VM so Meera can return to it later; it is a restore point, not a separate copy she can give to someone else.
Start only boots the VM up from where it left off; it creates nothing new.
Stop shuts the VM down cleanly; it does not produce a second copy of anything.

questions.q: A logistics company owns 10 physical servers. Each runs a single application and sits mostly idle, yet each needs its own power, cooling and space. The IT lead proposes replacing all of them with one powerful server running 10 VMs. Which reason for using hypervisors is this, and what is the payoff?
options: Safe Testing — risky updates can be tried without touching the real system
Server Consolidation — huge savings in cost and energy
Fast Disaster Recovery — a crashed VM is restored from a snapshot in minutes
Safe Isolation — if one VM crashes the others keep running
questions.explain: Server Consolidation is exactly this move: many under-used physical servers become one powerful machine running the same workloads as VMs. Because the hypervisor lets that one server use its full capacity, the company pays for and powers one box instead of ten. That is where the large cost and energy savings come from.
why_wrong: Safe Testing is about trying risky updates or new software in a VM without touching the real system; nothing here is being tested.
Fast Disaster Recovery is about restoring a crashed VM from a snapshot in minutes; no server has crashed in this scenario, the problem is idle hardware.
Safe Isolation is a benefit that will come along with the move, but the reason for doing it is to replace 10 idle servers with 1, which is consolidation.

questions.q: Cloud computing is often compared to using electricity from the grid rather than running your own generator. What does this analogy say about how cloud computing works?
options: You buy your own servers once, and the cloud provider then supplies only the electricity to keep them running.
The provider ships dedicated hardware to your building, which you own and operate yourself.
Instead of buying and maintaining your own servers, you rent computing power, storage and software over the Internet and pay for what you use.
You install and manage the hypervisor yourself, and the provider only hosts the storage for your virtual machines.
questions.explain: Nobody builds a power plant to run a fridge; you plug in and pay for the units you consume. Cloud computing works the same way: the provider owns and runs the servers, storage and software, and you rent them over the Internet and pay for what you actually use. That is what removes the cost and effort of buying and maintaining your own machines.
why_wrong: Buying your own servers is the on-premises 'generator' model the analogy argues against; in the cloud you rent the computing capacity itself, not just the power to run hardware you own.
Dedicated hardware that you own and run in your own building is on-premises computing, the opposite of plugging into a shared utility.
Cloud providers run millions of hypervisor-managed VMs in their own data centres; installing and managing the hypervisor is the provider's job, not yours.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five NIST characteristics that make a service genuinely 'cloud'?
questions.explain: The five NIST characteristics are On-Demand Self-Service, Broad Network Access, Resource Pooling, Rapid Elasticity and Measured Service. Virtualisation is the technology the cloud is built on, with providers running millions of hypervisor-managed VMs across giant data centres, but it is the foundation underneath the service, not one of the five traits used to judge whether a service is truly cloud.
why_wrong: Resource Pooling is one of the five NIST characteristics.
Measured Service is one of the five NIST characteristics; it is why a shopping site that scales up for a sale pays only for what it actually used.
Broad Network Access is one of the five NIST characteristics.

questions.q: In the 'Pizza as a Service' analogy, which service model corresponds to take-and-bake pizza?
questions.explain: With take-and-bake pizza someone else prepares the base, but you still have to bake it and finish it yourself. That matches IaaS: the provider supplies the servers, storage, networking and virtualisation, and you install the operating system, runtime and applications on top. The more the provider does for you, the further you move along the analogy toward dining at a restaurant.
why_wrong: SaaS is dining at a restaurant: the provider manages everything and you simply use the finished app.
PaaS is pizza delivery: the provider also manages the OS and runtime, and you only add your code.
On-Premises is making pizza at home: you buy the ingredients, own the oven and do everything yourself.

questions.q: Under the IaaS model, which of these layers is managed by the provider rather than by you?
questions.explain: In IaaS the provider takes care of the bottom four layers: virtualisation, servers, storage and networking. Everything above that, meaning the operating system, middleware, runtime, data and applications, is yours to install and maintain. Responsibility shifts further toward the provider only as you move up to PaaS and SaaS.
why_wrong: Runtime is managed by you under IaaS; it becomes the provider's responsibility only from PaaS upward.
Middleware is managed by you under IaaS; the provider takes it over only in PaaS and SaaS.
The operating system is managed by you under IaaS, which is why the take-and-bake analogy says you install the OS and apps yourself.

questions.q: A team migrates from IaaS to PaaS. Which one of these layers stops being their responsibility and becomes the provider's?
questions.explain: Moving from IaaS to PaaS hands three layers to the provider: the operating system, middleware and runtime. Applications and data stay with you in both models, and storage and networking were already the provider's under IaaS. That is why PaaS is 'pizza delivery': the base and the oven are handled, you only add your code.
why_wrong: Applications are managed by you under both IaaS and PaaS; only SaaS hands them to the provider.
Data is managed by you under both IaaS and PaaS; only SaaS hands it to the provider.
Storage and networking were already the provider's responsibility under IaaS, so nothing changes for them in the move.

questions.q: Which statement about the cloud infrastructure market (Q1 2026, Synergy Research) is correct?
options: Azure is the fastest-growing of the Big Three.
Google Cloud launched first and still leads the market.
AWS launched first, in 2006, and still leads the market.
The three largest providers together run less than half of the world's cloud infrastructure.
questions.explain: Amazon Web Services was the first of the big providers to launch, back in 2006, and it still holds the largest share. Just three companies run over 60% of the world's cloud infrastructure. Each of the three has its own profile: AWS leads, Azure's strength is its deep ties to enterprise Microsoft tools, and Google Cloud is the fastest-growing.
why_wrong: Google Cloud, not Azure, is the fastest-growing of the Big Three; Azure's distinguishing strength is its deep ties to enterprise Microsoft tools.
AWS, not Google Cloud, launched first and still leads; Google Cloud is the fastest-growing, not the largest.
Just three companies run over 60% of the world's cloud infrastructure, well over half.

questions.q: A university's exam-results portal gets almost no traffic all year, then millions of hits on results day. Hosted on a cloud provider, it automatically adds servers as the load spikes, drops them again by evening, and the month's bill reflects only the hours those extra servers actually ran. Which two NIST characteristics does this story show?
options: Resource Pooling and Broad Network Access
Rapid Elasticity and Broad Network Access
questions.explain: Adding servers as demand rises and removing them when it falls is Rapid Elasticity: capacity stretches and shrinks with the load. Being billed only for the hours the extra servers actually ran is Measured Service: usage is metered and you pay for what you consume. A shopping site scaling up for a big sale and paying only for what it used is exactly the same pattern.
why_wrong: Resource Pooling is about many customers sharing the provider's physical resources and Broad Network Access is about reaching the service from any device over the network; neither describes scaling with demand or paying per use.

On-Demand Self-Service is about provisioning resources yourself without waiting on the provider, and Resource Pooling is about shared infrastructure; the story is about automatic scaling and a usage-based bill.
Rapid Elasticity is half right, but Broad Network Access does not explain the pay-only-for-what-ran bill; that is Measured Service.

questions.q: At 2 a.m. before a demo, Sana logs into her cloud provider's web console, picks a VM size and clicks Create; the machine is running within a minute. She never raised a ticket, emailed anyone or waited for a person at the provider to approve the request. Which NIST characteristic does this most directly illustrate?
questions.explain: On-Demand Self-Service means a customer can provision computing resources such as a server or storage by themselves, whenever they need them, without any human interaction with the provider. Sana got a running VM in the middle of the night purely through the console, which is exactly that. It is the trait that makes renting computing power feel like flipping a switch rather than placing an order with a supplier and waiting.
why_wrong: Rapid Elasticity is about capacity growing and shrinking with demand; Sana created a single machine for a demo, and nothing in the story scales up or down with load.
Resource Pooling is about the provider serving many customers from shared physical resources; the story is about how Sana obtained the VM, not about whose hardware it shares.
Measured Service is about metering usage and paying for what you consume; no bill or usage measurement appears anywhere in the story.

questions.q: A hospital keeps its patient records on servers inside its own building because of privacy rules, but runs its public website and appointment-booking app on AWS. The two environments are connected so the booking app can check free slots against the internal system. Which deployment model is this?
questions.explain: A hybrid cloud is a connected mix of private and public: the sensitive part (patient records) stays on infrastructure dedicated to the hospital, while the public-facing apps run on a shared public cloud such as AWS. The link between the two is what makes it hybrid rather than two separate setups. This is the standard pattern for keeping sensitive data private while still using the public cloud for everything else.
why_wrong: A private cloud would mean everything, including the website and booking app, runs on infrastructure dedicated to the hospital alone; here the public-facing apps are on AWS.
A public cloud would put the patient records on shared AWS infrastructure too, which is exactly what the hospital is avoiding.
A community cloud is shared by several organisations with common needs, such as government agencies pooling infrastructure; the hospital is not sharing its systems with other organisations.

questions.q: Five state universities in the same region must all follow the same data-protection rules for student records. Instead of each building its own cloud, they set up one shared infrastructure that only these five universities use; no outside company can rent capacity on it. Which deployment model is this?
questions.explain: A community cloud is infrastructure shared by a group of organisations that have common needs; government agencies sharing one platform is the classic example. It sits between private (one organisation only) and public (open to anyone): the member organisations share it, but nobody outside the group can use it. Several universities with identical compliance needs pooling one infrastructure fits this exactly.
why_wrong: A public cloud is shared infrastructure open to anyone, like AWS, Azure or Google Cloud; here only the five universities can use it and outside companies are shut out.
A hybrid cloud is a connected mix of public and private infrastructure; nothing in this setup places any part on a public cloud.
A private cloud is dedicated to a single organisation, such as a bank's internal cloud; here five separate universities share the same infrastructure.

questions.q: Meera works in IT at a bank. Management wants developers to be able to spin up virtual machines on demand, but insists the infrastructure be used by the bank alone and never shared with any other company. Which deployment model should Meera propose?
questions.explain: A private cloud is dedicated to one organisation only; a bank's internal cloud is the classic example. It still delivers cloud-style conveniences such as self-service VMs, but on infrastructure nobody outside the bank uses. When the hard requirement is 'shared with no other company', private is the only model that fits.
why_wrong: A public cloud is shared infrastructure open to anyone, which is exactly what management has ruled out.
A community cloud is shared by several organisations with common needs; the bank does not want to share with anyone.
A hybrid cloud connects a private part to a public part; management wants nothing on shared public infrastructure, so there is no public half to connect.

questions.q: Arjun has finished a web app for a hackathon. He wants to push his code and have it run on the Internet without ever picking an operating system, installing a runtime or configuring a server. Which service model, and which example, fits what he wants?
options: PaaS, for example Google App Engine
IaaS, for example a rented virtual machine on AWS
On-Premises, running the app on his own laptop
questions.explain: Under PaaS the provider manages the runtime, middleware, operating system and everything below; you manage only your application and its data. That is precisely 'push code and the platform just runs it', which is what Google App Engine (or Heroku, or Azure App Service) offers. In pizza terms it is delivery: you add nothing but your code.
why_wrong: On an IaaS virtual machine Arjun would still have to install the operating system and runtime himself, which is exactly what he wants to avoid.
SaaS is a finished application you simply use, like Google Photos; it does not run code that Arjun writes.
Running on his own laptop means he manages all eight layers himself, including the OS and the server, the opposite of what he asked for.

questions.q: Priya's college design club signs up for a web-based video-calling service to hold weekly meetings. Nobody in the club installs software on a server, patches an operating system or manages a runtime; they open the app in a browser and use it. In pizza terms, what has the club chosen?
questions.explain: Dining at a restaurant means the provider does everything and you just enjoy the finished dish. That is SaaS: the provider manages all eight layers, from networking and servers up to the application itself, and the club simply uses the finished app. Zoom handling video calls for millions of simultaneous meetings is exactly this kind of service.
why_wrong: Take-and-bake (IaaS) would leave the club installing the OS and app on rented servers, which nobody in the club is doing.
Pizza delivery (PaaS) still requires you to bring your own code; the club is not writing or deploying any application.
Making pizza at home (On-Premises) means owning and managing every layer yourself, the opposite of using a hosted app in a browser.

questions.q: Rahul's team rents virtual machines from a cloud provider, installs Ubuntu on them and deploys their app. Months later the site is breached through a known operating-system vulnerability that was never patched. Under the model they were using, who was responsible for keeping the OS patched?
options: Rahul's team, because under IaaS the customer manages the operating system
The provider, because under IaaS the provider manages the operating system and everything below it
The provider, because the operating system is part of the virtualisation layer
Rahul's team is responsible only for applications and data; the OS was the provider's job
questions.explain: Renting VMs and installing your own OS is IaaS. In that model the provider's responsibility stops at virtualisation, servers, storage and networking; the operating system, middleware, runtime, data and applications are the customer's. So patching Ubuntu was Rahul's team's job. Had they wanted the provider to own the OS, they would have needed PaaS or SaaS.
why_wrong: Under IaaS the provider's responsibility stops below the OS, at virtualisation, servers, storage and networking; the OS is the customer's.
The operating system is its own layer above virtualisation; the provider manages the hypervisor and the VMs, not the OS installed inside them.
Managing only applications and data is the PaaS split; Rahul's team chose IaaS by installing their own OS, so the OS was theirs.

questions.q: In computational thinking, what does decomposition mean?
options: Breaking a complex problem into smaller, more manageable parts, solving each part, then combining the solutions
Focusing only on the details that matter and hiding everything else
Spotting similarities and repeats so an existing solution can be reused
Writing the exact, ordered steps that solve the problem
questions.explain: Decomposition is the act of splitting one big, tangled problem into smaller pieces that can each be handled on their own, after which the part-solutions are combined into the full solution. It is the first move in almost every computational thinking process because most real problems are too large to attack in one go. Small parts are less overwhelming, can be worked on in parallel by different people, and make mistakes easier to isolate.
why_wrong: Focusing on what matters and hiding the rest is abstraction, which reduces complexity rather than splitting the problem up.
Spotting similarities and repeats so a known solution can be reused is pattern recognition, which usually comes after the problem has been decomposed.
Writing the exact ordered steps is the algorithm stage, the concrete plan you write once decomposition, pattern recognition and abstraction are done.

questions.q: Which building block of computational thinking is described as focusing on what matters and ignoring the rest?
questions.explain: Abstraction means keeping only the details that matter for the problem at hand and hiding everything else. It lets you work with a simple model instead of every internal detail, which is why a driver only needs a steering wheel and pedals while the engine and transmission stay out of sight. Without it, nobody could hold a complex system in their head at once.
why_wrong: Decomposition breaks a big problem into smaller parts; it does not decide which details to hide.
Pattern recognition is about noticing similarities and repeats so a solution can be reused, not about hiding detail.
Algorithms are the finite, ordered steps that solve the problem once the thinking work is done.

questions.q: Which building block of computational thinking lets you reuse a solution that already worked instead of solving the same kind of problem from scratch?
questions.explain: Pattern recognition is noticing similarities, trends or repeats among problems and within a problem's parts. Once you see that a new problem resembles one you have already solved, you can apply the old solution instead of starting over, which saves time and turns a messy problem into a familiar one. Shape sequences, number series, sorting laundry and streaming recommendations all rely on it.
why_wrong: Abstraction reduces complexity by hiding unnecessary detail; reuse there comes from a stable simple interface, not from spotting repeats.
Decomposition splits a problem into parts; reuse only becomes visible once you look for patterns inside those parts.
Effectiveness is a trait of a good algorithm, meaning every step is practically executable, not a building block about reuse.

questions.q: An algorithm can be expressed in more than one form. Which of the following is one of those forms?
questions.explain: The same algorithm can be written as plain English, as a flowchart, as pseudocode, or as actual program code; the steps stay identical and only the form changes. A flowchart simply draws those ordered steps as boxes and arrows. This is why an algorithm can be shared and followed by any person or machine, whatever notation it is written in.
why_wrong: A star topology is a network layout showing devices connected to a central hub or switch, not a way of writing steps.
A file permission setting controls who may read, write or execute a file; it says nothing about the steps of a solution.
A virtual hard disk is the storage file a hypervisor creates for a virtual machine, unrelated to expressing an algorithm.

questions.q: The Input trait of a good algorithm allows how many inputs?
options: At least one input, never zero
questions.explain: The Input trait requires zero or more well-defined inputs, so an algorithm may legitimately take no input at all. An algorithm that simply prints the numbers 1 to 10 is still valid because what matters is that any inputs it does take are clearly defined. The stricter at-least-one rule belongs to Output, not Input.
why_wrong: Nothing restricts an algorithm to a single input; many algorithms take several well-defined inputs.
There is no minimum of two inputs; that number appears nowhere among the traits of a good algorithm.
Requiring at least one is the Output rule; inputs are allowed to be zero in number.

questions.q: Which trait of a good algorithm means that every step is clear and unambiguous?
questions.explain: Definiteness is the requirement that each step be stated so clearly that no two people, and no machine, could interpret it differently. Vague wording such as heat the water for a while breaks it, because two people following the instruction get different results. Clear steps are what make an algorithm repeatable by anyone who follows it.
why_wrong: Finiteness is about the algorithm stopping after a limited number of steps, not about how clearly each step is worded.
Effectiveness means each step is simple and practically doable in the real world, which is different from being clearly stated.
Output means the algorithm must produce at least one defined, useful result.

questions.q: What does the Finiteness trait of a good algorithm require?
options: That every step is practically executable
That it produces at least one useful output
That the algorithm terminates after a finite number of steps
That every step is clear and unambiguous
questions.explain: Finiteness means the algorithm must come to an end after a limited number of steps rather than running forever. A set of instructions that says to keep comparing values without ever saying when to stop fails this trait, because it never guarantees an answer. An algorithm that cannot terminate cannot be relied on to deliver a result at all.
why_wrong: Being practically executable is Effectiveness; a step can be perfectly doable and still repeat forever.
Producing at least one useful result is the Output trait, which an endless algorithm would never reach anyway.
Clear, unambiguous wording is Definiteness; an instruction can be perfectly clear and still never stop.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the four building blocks of computational thinking?
questions.explain: The four building blocks are decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction and algorithms. Algorithms is the last of them: the exact, ordered steps that turn the thinking work into something a person or machine can actually carry out. The other three prepare the problem so those steps can be written.
why_wrong: Virtualization is the technology that lets one physical machine run several virtual machines through a hypervisor.
Rapid elasticity is one of the five NIST characteristics of cloud computing, about scaling resources up and down on demand.
Topology is the layout of a computer network, such as star, bus, ring or mesh.

questions.q: Which operating system function decides which program gets the CPU, and for how long?
questions.explain: Process management is the scheduling job of the operating system: it decides which running program gets the processor and for how long before the next one gets a turn. This rapid sharing of one CPU is what makes multitasking appear to happen. Every other OS function depends on processes being given CPU time in an orderly way.
why_wrong: Memory management allocates and frees RAM so processes do not overwrite one another; it does not schedule CPU time.
File management organises data into files and folders and controls access to them.
Device management communicates with printers, disks and keyboards through drivers.

questions.q: Which operating system function allocates and frees RAM so that processes do not collide?
questions.explain: Memory management hands each running program the RAM it needs and reclaims that space when the program is finished. Keeping these allocations separate is what stops one process from writing over another's data. When you open an app, the memory manager reserves its RAM before the process manager can schedule it on the CPU.
why_wrong: Process management decides which program gets the CPU and for how long, not how RAM is divided up.
Security and access enforces logins, permissions and isolation between users.
The user interface function provides the GUI or command line you interact with.

questions.q: An operating system is compared to which everyday role, because it decides which part of the system gets a resource and when, so that nothing collides?
options: A compiler that translates source code
A router that directs traffic between networks
questions.explain: The air-traffic controller comparison captures the operating system's central job: the CPU, memory, storage, keyboard and every running app all want attention at once, and the OS decides who goes when. Like planes waiting for a runway, requests are sequenced so nothing crashes into anything else. Without that arbitration, every app would have to negotiate with the hardware directly.
why_wrong: A compiler turns source code into machine code; it is a development tool, not the manager of running resources.
A database stores and retrieves structured records and is an application, not the resource manager of the machine.
A router forwards data between different networks; it manages network traffic, not a computer's CPU, memory and devices.

questions.q: Which type of operating system guarantees a response within a strict time limit?
questions.explain: A real-time operating system is built so that a response is delivered inside a fixed deadline, every time. That guarantee is what makes it suitable for car airbags, pacemakers and industrial robots, where being late is the same as failing. FreeRTOS, VxWorks and QNX are examples of this type.
why_wrong: A batch OS gathers jobs and runs them in groups with no interaction, so it offers no timing guarantee at all.
A time-sharing OS switches the CPU rapidly between users' tasks for fairness, not to meet a hard deadline.
A distributed OS makes many computers look like a single system to the user; timing guarantees are not its purpose.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a Mobile OS?
questions.explain: HarmonyOS belongs to the mobile operating system family, along with Android, iOS and KaiOS. Mobile operating systems are built around touch input, battery life and an app ecosystem, which is what sets them apart from desktop and server systems. They run on phones, tablets and handhelds.
why_wrong: VxWorks is a real-time operating system used where a response must arrive inside a strict deadline.
Multics is a classic time-sharing operating system, designed to switch the CPU among many users' tasks.
Plan 9 from Bell Labs is a distributed operating system, which makes several machines appear as one system.

questions.q: Which type of operating system collects jobs and runs them in groups, with no direct interaction while they run?
questions.explain: A batch operating system gathers work into batches and processes them together without anyone sitting at a terminal guiding it. Results appear once the batch has finished rather than moment by moment. Early bank cheque processing worked this way, and systems such as IBM OS/360, z/OS and Unisys MCP are examples.
why_wrong: A mobile OS is built for touch input, battery life and app ecosystems on phones and tablets, which is interaction-heavy by design.
A real-time OS guarantees a response inside a strict time limit, as needed by pacemakers and airbags.
A distributed OS spreads work over many machines while presenting them to the user as a single system.

questions.q: Which operating system is the one used on Apple desktops and laptops?
questions.explain: macOS is Apple's operating system for its desktop and laptop computers, and it is widely associated with creative work. Knowing which OS family belongs on which class of machine matters because each family is built around a different set of users and devices. Windows, Linux and Android occupy the other everyday slots.
why_wrong: Linux dominates servers, cloud infrastructure and supercomputers rather than Apple desktop hardware.
Android is a mobile operating system for smartphones and tablets.
Windows is the operating system found on personal and office computers worldwide.

questions.q: What does the pwd command do?
options: Lists the files and folders in the current directory
Prints the working directory, the folder you are currently in
Displays the contents of a file
questions.explain: pwd stands for print working directory and it reports the folder the terminal is currently sitting in. Because the Linux file system is one large tree starting at /, knowing exactly where you are is the first thing you check before creating, copying or deleting anything. Typing pwd in a fresh session might print something like /home/student.
why_wrong: Listing the files and folders in the current directory is what ls does.
Moving into another folder is the job of cd, short for change directory.
Displaying a file's contents in the terminal is what cat does.

questions.q: Which command shows the files and folders inside the current directory?
questions.explain: ls is short for list and prints the names of the files and folders in the directory you are in. It is one of the five navigation commands you type most, alongside pwd, cd, mkdir and rmdir. Giving it a folder name, as in ls labs, lists the contents of that folder instead.
why_wrong: mkdir creates a new folder; it shows you nothing about what already exists.
chmod changes a file's permissions, such as making a script executable.
rmdir deletes an empty folder rather than listing anything.

questions.q: In the Linux file system hierarchy, which directory holds essential user command binaries?
questions.explain: /bin holds the essential command binaries, the executable programs behind the basic commands every user needs. Because Linux keeps everything in one tree under /, each top-level directory has a defined purpose like this. Knowing these purposes is what lets you guess where an unfamiliar file belongs.
why_wrong: /var stores variable data such as logs and caches, which is where you look when a service is misbehaving.
/home contains the personal folders of the ordinary users on the system.
/usr contains installed programs and libraries rather than the essential base commands.

questions.q: Which Linux directory contains a personal folder for each user?
questions.explain: /home is where each ordinary user gets their own personal folder, so a user named student would work inside /home/student. Keeping personal files in one place per user is what lets the operating system enforce permissions between accounts. The administrator is the exception, with a separate home folder at /root.
why_wrong: /etc holds system-wide configuration files that apply to the whole machine.
/bin holds the essential command binaries used by all users.
/var holds logs, caches and other data that changes as the system runs.

questions.q: In Linux, every file and folder lives in one tree that starts at which directory?
questions.explain: The single forward slash / is the root of the Linux file system, and every other directory hangs somewhere below it. This is why Linux has no separate drive letters: one tree covers all storage. /bin, /etc, /home, /var, /usr and /root are all branches of that one tree.
why_wrong: /home is only the branch holding users' personal folders, not the top of the tree.
/root is the administrator's personal home folder, which sits below / and should not be confused with it.
/usr is the branch holding installed programs and libraries.

questions.q: Which Linux command removes an empty folder?
questions.explain: rmdir stands for remove directory and deletes a folder, provided that folder is already empty. It is one of the five everyday navigation commands, the counterpart to mkdir. If the folder still contains files, rmdir refuses and the contents must be dealt with first.
why_wrong: rm deletes files rather than folders.
mkdir creates a new folder; it is the opposite operation.
mv moves a file or folder to another location, or renames it, but never deletes it.

questions.q: Which Linux command deletes a file?
questions.explain: rm is the file management command that deletes a file. It sits alongside touch, cp, mv, cat and chmod in the set of commands used to create, copy, move, view and control files. Because there is no recycle bin in the terminal, a file removed with rm is gone, which is why the exact filename matters.
why_wrong: rmdir removes an empty folder, not a file.
cp makes a copy of a file or folder, leaving the original in place.
touch creates a new empty file rather than removing one.

questions.q: In computer networking, what does the term 'topology' refer to?
options: The physical or logical layout of how devices are connected
The maximum number of devices a network is allowed to hold
The speed at which data travels across the network
The geographical area a network covers
questions.explain: Topology is the arrangement of a network: how the devices are wired or logically linked to one another. Star, bus, ring and mesh are the four common layouts. Two networks can carry the same data at the same speed and still have completely different topologies, because topology describes shape, not performance.
why_wrong: How many devices a network supports is a capacity limit, not a description of how those devices are arranged.
Speed is a measure of bandwidth and performance; a star and a ring network can run at identical speeds.
Geographical area is what the PAN, LAN, MAN and WAN classification describes, which is a separate way of sorting networks.

questions.q: Which type of network covers a single building or campus, such as a college computer lab?
questions.explain: A LAN links the devices inside one building or campus so they can share files, printers and an internet connection. A college computer lab, an office floor and a hostel's Wi-Fi are all LANs. The defining feature is the limited physical area it serves, not the number of machines on it.
why_wrong: A PAN spans only a few metres and links one person's own devices, such as earbuds paired to a phone.
A MAN spans a whole city, for example a city's cable-TV or traffic-camera network.
A WAN spans countries or continents; the Internet itself is the largest example.

questions.q: Which network device allows wireless devices to join a wired network?
questions.explain: An access point is the bridge between the wireless world and a wired network: it receives Wi-Fi signals from phones and laptops and passes that traffic onto the cabled network. This is what lets devices with no Ethernet port become full members of the same network. Many home routers include an access point built in, which is why one box seems to do both jobs.
why_wrong: A NIC is the hardware inside a single device that connects that one device to a network; it does not let other devices join.
A modem converts signals between your ISP and your network; it is the link to the outside world, not a way to add wireless clients.
A hub connects devices within one small network by broadcasting to all of them, and it works over cables, not wirelessly.

questions.q: In which network topology does each device connect directly to many or all of the other devices?
questions.explain: In a mesh topology the devices are linked to one another directly, often with many redundant paths. That redundancy is its strength: if one link fails, traffic can still reach its destination another way. The trade-off is the large number of connections needed as devices are added.
why_wrong: In a star topology every device connects to one central hub or switch rather than to the other devices.
In a bus topology all devices share a single central cable instead of having direct links to each other.
In a ring topology each device connects to exactly two neighbours, forming a closed loop.

questions.q: Which device converts signals between your Internet Service Provider and your own network?
questions.explain: The modem sits at the boundary of your home, translating the signal that arrives on the ISP's line into something your network equipment understands, and back again. Without it, the line from the ISP cannot be used by your devices at all. In a typical home the chain runs Internet (ISP) to modem to router to your devices.
why_wrong: A switch connects devices within one network and forwards data only to the intended device; it does no signal conversion for the ISP line.
A router directs traffic between different networks and finds the best path, but it relies on the modem to reach the ISP.
An access point lets wireless devices join a wired network; it adds Wi-Fi coverage rather than translating the ISP's signal.

questions.q: Which type of network spans countries or continents, with the Internet itself as the classic example?
questions.explain: A WAN is the largest of the four size categories, linking networks across countries and continents. The Internet is the WAN everyone uses every day. Data travelling from your laptop to a server abroad crosses a LAN first, then leaves through your router onto the WAN.
why_wrong: A MAN covers a single city, such as a municipal cable-TV or traffic-camera network.
A LAN is confined to one building or campus, like a computer lab or an office.
A PAN reaches only a few metres and links one person's own devices.

questions.q: How does a hub deliver data that arrives for a device on its network?
options: It broadcasts the data to every connected device
It sends the data only to the device it is meant for
It chooses the best path to a different network
It converts the data between the ISP's signal and the network's signal
questions.explain: A hub has no intelligence about which port a particular device is on, so it simply repeats incoming data out to everyone attached. Every machine receives the traffic and ignores what is not addressed to it, which wastes bandwidth and causes collisions. That is why hubs have largely been replaced by switches.
why_wrong: Sending data only to the intended device is what a switch does; that selectivity is exactly what a hub lacks.
Choosing the best path to another network is the router's job, and it requires intelligence a hub does not have.
Converting between the ISP's signal and the network's signal is the modem's function.

questions.q: Which network device directs traffic between different networks, for example between a home network and the Internet?
questions.explain: A router's job is to move traffic from one network to another and to work out the best path for it. This is what connects your home network to the wider Internet. Its scope is what distinguishes it: it operates between networks rather than inside a single one.
why_wrong: A switch works within one network, intelligently forwarding data between devices on that same network.
A hub also works within one small network, and it simply broadcasts to every device rather than routing anything.
A NIC is the hardware inside one device that attaches that device to a network; it makes no forwarding decisions between networks.

questions.q: What is a virtual machine?
options: A computer built entirely in software, with its own virtual CPU, memory, disk and operating system
A physical server that has been dedicated to running one application
A program that makes an existing operating system run faster
A backup copy of a computer's files kept on a second disk
questions.explain: A virtual machine is a computer inside a computer: the hypervisor hands it virtual hardware, and a full operating system installs and runs on that virtual hardware. To the software inside, it looks and behaves exactly like a real machine. Because it is only software, it can be created, copied and deleted without touching the physical computer.
why_wrong: A dedicated physical server is real hardware; virtualisation exists precisely to avoid tying one application to one physical box.
A VM does not speed anything up; it adds a software layer so that several operating systems can share one machine.
A backup stores copies of files, while a VM is a running machine with its own CPU, memory, disk and OS.

questions.q: Which virtual machine management action permanently removes the VM and frees the resources it was using?
questions.explain: Delete destroys the virtual machine and returns its allocated disk, memory and CPU share to the host. It is the only one of the management actions that is permanent, so it is used when a VM is genuinely no longer needed. Everything else on the list leaves the VM in place.
why_wrong: Stop only shuts the VM down cleanly; the VM and its virtual disk remain and can be started again later.
Snapshot saves the VM's exact state so it can be returned to later, which is the opposite of removing it.
Clone creates an identical second copy of the VM, so it adds a machine rather than freeing resources.

questions.q: A Type 1 hypervisor is also known by which name?
questions.explain: Type 1 hypervisors are called bare-metal because they install directly onto the physical hardware with no host operating system beneath them. Removing that extra layer is what makes them fast, which is why data centres use them. VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V, Citrix Hypervisor and KVM are the standard examples.
why_wrong: Hosted is the name for a Type 2 hypervisor, which runs as an application on top of an existing operating system.
Guest refers to an operating system running inside a virtual machine, not to a category of hypervisor.
Snapshot is a VM management action that saves a machine's state; it is not a kind of hypervisor.

questions.q: When creating a new virtual machine, what do you attach so that the guest operating system can be installed?
options: A snapshot taken from another VM
The host machine's own operating system
questions.explain: A blank virtual machine has virtual hardware but no software on it, so it needs installation media just like a real computer would. Attaching an ISO image of the operating system lets the VM boot from it and run the installer. After the install finishes, the VM boots from its own virtual hard disk instead.
why_wrong: A snapshot restores a machine to a state it was already in; it is not installation media for a fresh VM.
Driver packages help an operating system talk to hardware, but they cannot install the operating system itself.
The host's operating system stays on the host; the guest needs its own copy installed inside the VM.

questions.q: Which virtual machine action saves the VM's exact current state so you can return to it later?
questions.explain: A snapshot records the state of the virtual machine at a moment in time, so the VM can be rolled back to exactly that point later. It is the usual safety net before a risky change, because undoing the change becomes a matter of restoring the snapshot. The VM keeps running normally after the snapshot is taken.
why_wrong: Clone produces a separate identical copy of the whole VM, which is for duplicating a machine rather than for returning the original to an earlier state.
Stop shuts the VM down cleanly; it ends the session but records no state you can roll back to.
Start boots the VM up from where it left off and saves nothing.

questions.q: Which of these is a Type 2 (hosted) hypervisor?
questions.explain: Oracle VirtualBox installs like an ordinary application on top of Windows, macOS or Linux, which is exactly what makes it Type 2. Hosted hypervisors are simple to set up and are the usual choice for a student who wants to try another operating system on a personal laptop. VMware Workstation, VMware Fusion and Parallels Desktop belong in the same group.
why_wrong: VMware ESXi is a Type 1 bare-metal hypervisor installed directly on server hardware.
Microsoft Hyper-V is a Type 1 bare-metal hypervisor used in data centres.
KVM is a Type 1 bare-metal hypervisor, not an application layered on a host OS.

questions.q: Restoring a crashed virtual machine from a snapshot in minutes rather than days is which company benefit of using hypervisors?
questions.explain: Because a VM is just software plus saved state, recovering one means restoring a snapshot instead of rebuilding a physical machine and reinstalling everything. That turns a multi-day outage into a few minutes of work. It is one of the main reasons businesses virtualise their servers.
why_wrong: Server consolidation is about replacing many under-used physical servers with one machine running many VMs, saving cost and energy.
Safe testing is about trying risky updates or unknown software inside a VM so the real system is never touched.
Better utilisation refers to using a physical server's full capacity instead of leaving it idle.

questions.q: Which cloud deployment model uses shared infrastructure that is open to anyone, with AWS, Azure and Google Cloud as its examples?
questions.explain: In a public cloud the provider owns huge pools of hardware and rents capacity to any customer who signs up, so the underlying infrastructure is shared among many unrelated organisations. This sharing is what makes it cheap and instantly available. AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud are the best known public clouds.
why_wrong: A private cloud is dedicated to one organisation alone, such as a bank's internal cloud, and is not open to outside customers.
A hybrid cloud is a connected mix of public and private infrastructure, typically keeping sensitive data private while running apps publicly.
A community cloud is shared only by a set of organisations with common needs, such as several government agencies, rather than by anyone.

questions.q: In the 'Pizza as a Service' analogy, pizza delivery represents which cloud service model?
questions.explain: With pizza delivery someone else does the cooking and brings it to your table, but you still supply the table and eat it yourself. That matches PaaS, where the provider manages the servers, operating system and runtime and you supply only your code. Google App Engine is a typical example.
why_wrong: IaaS is the take-and-bake pizza: the provider gives you servers and storage, but you still install the operating system and applications.
SaaS is dining at a restaurant, where the provider manages everything and you simply use the finished application.
On-premises is making the pizza at home: you buy the ingredients, own the oven and do every part yourself.

questions.q: Which cloud characteristic describes resources being added automatically as demand rises and removed again as demand falls?
questions.explain: Rapid elasticity is the cloud's ability to grow and shrink with the workload almost instantly. A service can scale out for a traffic spike and scale back down afterwards without anyone buying or retiring hardware. It is one of the five characteristics that make a service genuinely cloud.
why_wrong: Resource pooling is the provider serving many customers from one shared pool of hardware, which is about sharing rather than scaling up and down.
Broad network access means the service is reachable over the network from many kinds of device.
On-demand self-service means you can provision resources yourself without a human at the provider approving the request.

questions.q: The five characteristics used to define genuine cloud computing come from which organisation?
questions.explain: The five traits of cloud computing are the NIST definition, the standard reference used almost everywhere. They are on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service. A service that misses one of them is usually not considered true cloud computing.
why_wrong: IEEE publishes many computing and networking standards, but the five cloud characteristics are not its definition.
ISO issues international standards across many industries; the widely quoted list of five cloud traits does not come from it.
W3C sets standards for the World Wide Web, such as HTML and CSS, not the definition of cloud computing.

questions.q: Among the Big Three cloud providers, which one is described as the fastest growing?
questions.explain: Google Cloud holds the smallest share of the Big Three but is expanding its share of global cloud infrastructure spending the quickest. AWS, Azure and Google Cloud together account for more than 60% of that spending. Fastest growing is about the rate of change, not the size of the share.
why_wrong: AWS launched first, in 2006, and still leads the market, but leading is not the same as growing fastest.
Azure is second by market share and is known for its deep ties to enterprise Microsoft tools rather than for the fastest growth.
IBM Cloud is not one of the Big Three that dominate global cloud infrastructure spending.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of cloud computing?
options: Google Photos storing and syncing billions of photos across all of a user's devices
A pacemaker running a real-time operating system to guarantee response times
VirtualBox installed on a student's laptop to run one Linux virtual machine
A ring topology connecting each office computer to exactly two neighbours
questions.explain: Cloud computing means using computing power, storage and software owned and run by a provider and reached over the Internet. Google Photos fits exactly: the photos live in the provider's data centres and every device reaches the same library over the network. Netflix on AWS, Dropbox and Zoom are further examples of the same idea.
why_wrong: A pacemaker runs a real-time operating system on its own embedded hardware, with no rented resources reached over the Internet.
VirtualBox on a laptop is personal virtualisation using hardware the student already owns; nothing is rented over a network.
A ring topology is a way of laying out a local network's connections and has nothing to do with renting computing resources.

questions.q: Under the SaaS model, who manages the application itself?
options: The provider, so the customer only uses the finished application
The customer, while the provider supplies only servers and storage
The customer, while the provider manages only the stored data
Nobody, because SaaS applications need no management at all
questions.explain: SaaS sits at the top of the stack: the provider handles the servers, storage, virtualisation, operating system, runtime, data and the application itself. The customer's only job is to open the app and use it. That is why the analogy for SaaS is dining at a restaurant rather than cooking.
why_wrong: A provider supplying only servers and storage while the customer handles the software describes IaaS, not SaaS.
Under SaaS the provider manages the applications and the data layer, so this reverses the actual split of responsibility.
Every service needs management; in SaaS that work simply moves entirely to the provider instead of disappearing.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes abstraction from decomposition?
options: Decomposition breaks a problem into smaller parts that can be solved separately, while abstraction keeps only the details that matter and hides the rest
Decomposition hides the details that do not matter, while abstraction splits a problem into parts that different people can work on
They name the same skill; abstraction is simply the word used when the problem involves software
Decomposition applies only to computing problems, while abstraction applies only to everyday problems
questions.explain: Decomposition is about size: one big problem becomes several smaller ones that are solved and then recombined. Abstraction is about detail: out of everything that could be described, you keep only what matters and hide the rest, the way a car's dashboard hides fuel injection and gear ratios. They are separate moves, and most real solutions use both.
why_wrong: This swaps the two: hiding unnecessary detail is abstraction, and splitting a problem into separately solvable parts is decomposition.
They are two different blocks with two different jobs, and both are used far outside software — in cooking, sport, research and business.
Both work everywhere: decomposition is used on a tech fest or a room to be cleaned, and abstraction on ATMs, remotes and maps.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the reasons given for why computational thinking is needed?
options: It handles real complexity — problems like traffic, pandemics and recommendation systems are too big to solve by gut feeling
It makes thinking clearer — a vague, messy problem becomes a clear set of steps anyone can follow and check
It works everywhere — the same skills apply to cooking, sports, research, business and code
It guarantees that any solution built this way will be free of mistakes
questions.explain: The three reasons offered are handling real complexity, making thinking clearer, and working everywhere. Nothing about computational thinking guarantees correctness — a decomposed, patterned, abstracted solution can still be wrong, which is exactly why an algorithm is then checked against traits such as definiteness and finiteness. What the approach gives you is a structure in which mistakes are easier to find, not an absence of mistakes.
why_wrong: Handling real complexity is one of the three stated reasons: modern problems are too big for gut feeling alone.
Making thinking clearer is a stated reason: it turns a messy problem into ordered steps others can follow and verify.
Working everywhere is a stated reason: the same four skills apply well outside programming.

questions.q: Three of the following are used as examples of pattern recognition. Which one is NOT?
options: Matching socks by colour and size while pairing laundry
Netflix and Spotify suggesting what you might watch or hear next
Pressing volume up on a TV remote without thinking about the infrared codes underneath
Dr John Snow mapping cholera cases and seeing them cluster around one water pump
questions.explain: Pattern recognition means spotting similarities, trends or repeats so a known solution can be reused — sock pairing, streaming recommendations and Snow's cholera map all work that way. The TV remote is an abstraction example instead: one button hides the infrared signal, the binary code and the TV's microprocessor decoding it. Telling which block an example belongs to is the skill being tested here.
why_wrong: Pairing socks by colour and size is pattern recognition: you match on a recognised similarity instead of testing every possible pair.
Streaming recommendations are pattern recognition applied to data: repeats in what you watch or hear predict what comes next.
Snow's 1854 map is the classic pattern recognition case: a cluster in the data revealed the outbreak's source.

questions.q: A good and a flawed version of a tea-making algorithm are compared. Which of these steps belongs to the flawed version?
options: Add tea and wait until it feels ready
Add 1 tea bag and steep for 3 minutes
questions.explain: "Until it feels ready" is not something two people would carry out the same way, so the algorithm loses definiteness. The good version replaces every vague phrase with a measured quantity or a fixed time — 200 ml, one tea bag, three minutes — so anyone following it gets the same result. A step that depends on a feeling cannot be followed by a machine at all.
why_wrong: Boiling a stated 200 ml is precise and repeatable, which is exactly what the good version does.
One tea bag and three minutes fixes both the quantity and the time, leaving nothing open to interpretation.
Stir and serve is a clear final action that also gives the process a definite stopping point.

questions.q: Which pairing of a trait of a good algorithm with its meaning is correct?
options: Definiteness — the algorithm must terminate after a finite number of steps
Effectiveness — every step must be simple and practically executable
Finiteness — every step must be clear and unambiguous
Output — the algorithm must accept at least one well-defined input
questions.explain: Effectiveness asks whether a step can actually be carried out in practice: counting every grain of rice in a store room by hand is perfectly precise yet not effective. Definiteness is about the clarity of each step, finiteness about the process ending, and the output trait about producing at least one defined, useful result. Inputs are different again — an algorithm may have zero or more of them.
why_wrong: Terminating after a finite number of steps is finiteness; definiteness is about each step being clear and unambiguous.
Being clear and unambiguous is definiteness; finiteness is the requirement that the algorithm eventually stops.
The output trait requires at least one defined, useful result; inputs may number zero or more.

questions.q: The steps of the find-the-largest-number algorithm are shuffled: (P) if the next number is bigger, it becomes the new largest; (Q) assume the first number is the largest so far; (R) the value left is the largest number; (S) repeat until every number has been checked; (T) look at the next number in the list. Which order is correct?
questions.explain: You must begin with an assumption — treat the first number as the largest so far — because otherwise the first comparison has nothing to compare against. Then you look at the next number, replace the largest if that number is bigger, and repeat the look-and-compare until the list is exhausted; whatever value remains is the answer. Order is part of what makes a sequence of steps an algorithm rather than a pile of instructions.
why_wrong: This looks at the next number before anything has been assumed to be the largest, so the first comparison has no reference value.
This compares (P) before ever looking at a next number (T), so there is no second value in hand at the moment of comparison.
This starts by looking and comparing and only then sets the starting assumption, which is backwards.

questions.q: For a washing machine, which of the following is part of what the user sees and controls, rather than the complexity that is abstracted away?
options: How the machine controls the water level and the temperature
Selecting the wash program and pressing Start
How the motor rotates the drum and spins the clothes
How the sensors and control system manage timing, rinsing and draining
questions.explain: Abstraction splits a system into a small visible interface and a large hidden mechanism. On a washing machine the visible side is loading clothes and detergent, choosing a program, pressing Start and taking the clothes out again; water control, motors, sensors and timing all sit behind that interface. Being able to say which side of the line a detail falls on is what using abstraction means in practice.
why_wrong: Water level and temperature control is internal machinery hidden from the user, not something on the control panel.
Drum rotation and spin are handled by the motor and its electronics, entirely out of the user's sight.
Timing, rinsing and draining are managed by sensors and the control system; the user only sees the cycle finish.

questions.q: Which pairing of an operating system function with its job is correct?
options: Process management — allocates and frees RAM so that programs do not collide
Device management — enforces logins, permissions and user isolation
File management — organises data into files and folders and controls access to them
Memory management — decides which program gets the CPU, and for how long
questions.explain: File management is the function that structures stored data into files and folders and decides who may open what. Process management schedules the CPU, memory management hands out and reclaims RAM, and device management talks to printers, disks and keyboards through drivers. Each of the six functions is a different slice of the one job every OS exists to do: managing resources.
why_wrong: Allocating and freeing RAM is memory management; process management decides which program runs on the CPU and for how long.
Logins, permissions and user isolation belong to the security function; device management deals with hardware through drivers.
Deciding which program gets the CPU is process management; memory management is what allocates and frees RAM.

questions.q: Plan 9 from Bell Labs, Google Fuchsia and Amoeba are given as examples of which type of operating system?
questions.explain: A distributed OS makes several separate computers appear to users and programs as one single system, which is how very large data-centre platforms are run. Plan 9, Fuchsia and Amoeba are the named members of that family. Each of the other types solves a different problem and carries its own example list.
why_wrong: A batch OS collects jobs and runs them in groups with no interaction; IBM z/OS, OS/360 and Unisys MCP are its examples.
A real-time OS guarantees a response inside a strict time limit; FreeRTOS, VxWorks and QNX are its examples.
A time-sharing OS switches the CPU rapidly between many users' tasks; UNIX, Multics and Linux are its examples.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a Batch OS from a Time-Sharing OS?
options: A batch OS collects jobs and runs them in groups with no direct interaction, while a time-sharing OS switches the CPU rapidly between several users' tasks
A batch OS switches the CPU rapidly between users, while a time-sharing OS runs collected jobs overnight in one block
A batch OS guarantees a response within a strict time limit, while a time-sharing OS makes many machines look like one
A batch OS is built for touch and battery life, while a time-sharing OS runs only on single-user desktops
questions.explain: The dividing line is interaction. A batch system gathers jobs and runs them as a group with nobody sitting at a terminal, which is how early cheque processing worked; a time-sharing system slices the CPU between many users so each feels they have the machine to themselves, which is what a multi-user UNIX or Linux server does.
why_wrong: This is the two definitions swapped: rapid switching between users is time-sharing, and grouped non-interactive jobs are batch.
Guaranteeing a response inside a time limit describes a real-time OS, and making many computers look like one describes a distributed OS.
Touch and battery life describe a mobile OS, and time-sharing exists precisely to serve many users at once rather than one.

questions.q: After the OS has located a program file on disk, the remaining steps of opening the app are shuffled: (P) the process manager schedules it on the CPU; (Q) the memory manager allocates RAM for it; (R) the user interface draws the app's window; (S) the OS checks permissions to run it. Which order is correct?
questions.explain: A program needs somewhere to live before it can be given processor time, so RAM is allocated first and the process manager then schedules it on the CPU. The permission check follows, and drawing the window is the last step — which is why the app appears on screen only after disk access, memory allocation, scheduling and permission checks have all already happened, usually in well under a second.
why_wrong: Scheduling the program on the CPU before any RAM has been allocated puts process management ahead of memory management.
This begins with the permission check, but memory allocation and CPU scheduling come before it in the sequence described.
This inserts the permission check between memory allocation and CPU scheduling, which is not where it falls.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a mobile operating system?
questions.explain: Mobile operating systems are built around touch input, battery life and app ecosystems, and Android, iOS, HarmonyOS and KaiOS are the named members of that family. QNX belongs with FreeRTOS and VxWorks as a real-time OS, used where a response must be guaranteed inside a strict time limit, such as in vehicles and industrial equipment. The two families are judged by completely different requirements.
why_wrong: Android is a mobile OS, running on the majority of the world's smartphones and tablets.
HarmonyOS is a mobile OS, designed for phones and other handheld devices.
KaiOS is a mobile OS, aimed at lightweight feature phones.

questions.q: Which operating system and typical use pairing is INCORRECT?
options: Linux — servers, cloud infrastructure and supercomputers
macOS — Apple desktops and laptops, often for creative work
Windows — personal and office computers worldwide
Android and iOS — bare-metal software installed on data-centre servers to host virtual machines
questions.explain: Android and iOS are mobile operating systems for phones and tablets, built around touch, battery life and app stores. Software installed directly on bare data-centre servers to host virtual machines is a Type 1 hypervisor such as VMware ESXi or Hyper-V, which is a different kind of product altogether. The other three pairings name the usual homes of those OS families.
why_wrong: Linux really does run most web servers, cloud platforms and supercomputers, so this pairing is correct.
macOS runs on Apple desktops and laptops and is widely used for creative work, so this pairing is correct.
Windows is the usual choice on personal and office computers worldwide, so this pairing is correct.

questions.q: Why is an operating system compared to an air-traffic controller?
options: The CPU, memory, storage and every running app all want the machine at once, and the OS decides who goes when so nothing collides
The OS translates each program into machine code before allowing it to start
The OS keeps a permanent record of every program that has ever run, the way a tower logs flights
The OS lets each application speak directly to the hardware, so no coordination is needed
questions.explain: Every function of an OS radiates from one job: managing resources that many things want at the same time. Like planes queuing for a single runway, processes compete for the CPU, for RAM, for the disk and for the screen, and the OS sequences them so nothing collides. Remove that coordination and there is no multitasking, no shared screen and no file system.
why_wrong: Turning source code into machine code is a compiler's job, not part of the OS's resource management.
Logging is a minor side activity; the comparison is about live coordination of competing demands, not record keeping.
Apps talking straight to hardware is the situation without an OS — it is the problem the OS exists to solve, not what it does.

questions.q: Which pairing of a Linux directory with what it holds is correct?
questions.explain: /bin holds the essential command binaries a user runs, which is why the basic commands work even on a bare system. /var holds logs, caches and other data that changes as the system runs, /usr holds installed programs and libraries, /home holds one personal folder per user, and system-wide configuration lives in /etc. All of them hang off the single root, /.
why_wrong: /var holds logs, caches and variable data; installed programs and libraries live in /usr.
/usr holds installed programs and libraries; personal folders for each user live in /home.
/home holds users' personal folders; system-wide configuration files live in /etc.

questions.q: A short terminal session sets up a small project folder and two files inside it. Which order of commands does that correctly: (P) cd project, (Q) touch app.py notes.txt, (R) pwd, (S) mkdir project?
questions.explain: You check where you are with pwd, create the folder with mkdir project, move into it with cd project, and only then create the files with touch so they land inside the new folder. mkdir does not move you into the folder it creates, which is why the cd step is not optional. Running touch too early leaves app.py and notes.txt sitting in the parent folder.
why_wrong: cd project would fail here because the folder has not been created yet; mkdir has to come first.
This creates the two files before moving into project, so app.py and notes.txt end up outside the new folder.
This creates the files before the folder exists at all, leaving them beside project rather than inside it.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes what touch and mkdir each create?
options: touch creates a new folder, and mkdir creates an empty file inside it
touch creates an empty file, and mkdir creates a new folder
Both create empty files; mkdir simply also sets the file's permissions
touch copies an existing file into the current folder, and mkdir moves a file into a folder
questions.explain: touch makes an empty file, which is how app.py or notes.txt come into existence before there is anything to put in them. mkdir makes a directory, a container for files, and it leaves you exactly where you were — entering the new directory still takes cd. Copying and moving belong to cp and mv, and permissions are changed with chmod.
why_wrong: This swaps them: making folders is mkdir's job and making empty files is touch's.
mkdir does not create files at all, and changing permissions is done with chmod.
Copying a file is cp and moving or renaming one is mv; neither touch nor mkdir does either.

questions.q: Which statement about the Linux file system hierarchy is correct?
