options: Each storage device gets its own separate tree, so there is no single starting point
The tree starts at /root, and every other folder is created inside it
The tree starts at /home, and the system folders branch off each user's folder
Everything lives in one tree that starts at the root, written /
questions.explain: Linux organises all files and folders into a single tree whose top is written as one forward slash. Everything else — /bin, /etc, /home, /var, /usr, /root — is a branch of that root, which is why any location can be written as a path starting from /. The similar-looking /root is not the top of the tree; it is only the administrator's personal folder.
why_wrong: A single unified tree is the whole point of the Linux layout: there is exactly one starting point, /.
/root is the administrator's home folder, not the top of the tree; it sits under / alongside the other directories.
/home holds users' personal folders and is itself a branch of /; system folders such as /etc and /bin sit beside it, not inside it.

questions.q: Where does an ordinary user's personal folder live, and where does the administrator's home folder live?
options: Both sit under /home; the administrator's is /home/root
The user's is under /home, for example /home/student, and the administrator's is /root
The user's is under /usr and the administrator's is under /etc
The user's is under /home and the administrator's is under /bin
questions.explain: Each ordinary user gets a personal folder inside /home, which is why a student's terminal often opens at a path such as /home/student. The administrator has a separate home folder, /root, placed directly under the root of the tree rather than among the ordinary users. The names look alike, but / is the root of the whole tree while /root is just one folder in it.
why_wrong: The administrator's home is /root, directly under the root of the tree, not a folder inside /home.
/usr holds installed programs and libraries and /etc holds system-wide configuration; neither is anybody's home folder.
/bin holds essential command binaries, not the administrator's personal files.

questions.q: Which of these commands changes the directory you are currently working in?
questions.explain: cd, short for change directory, is the only one of the four that moves you: after cd project, pwd reports the new path. pwd and ls only report — one prints where you are, the other lists what is there. mkdir creates a folder but leaves you standing where you were, which is why making a folder and entering it takes two separate commands.
why_wrong: pwd, print working directory, prints the folder you are already in and never moves you.
ls lists the files and folders in the current directory without changing it.
mkdir creates a new folder but does not move you into it; cd is still needed afterwards.

questions.q: Which command lists what is inside a folder named labs while leaving you in the folder you are already in?
questions.explain: ls lists the contents of a directory, and giving it a name lists that directory instead of the current one, so ls labs shows what is inside labs without moving you. cd would change your working directory, so you would no longer be where you started. Commands that accept a target this way let you ask about a folder you are not standing in.
why_wrong: cd labs moves you into the folder, so your working directory changes and you would still need a separate command to see the contents.
cat displays the contents of a file, not a listing of a folder.
pwd takes no target at all; it simply prints the directory you are currently in.

questions.q: A computer network is described as serving three purposes. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
options: Sharing one printer or one internet line among everyone connected
Making files and databases reachable from any connected device
Automatically encrypting every file stored on each connected computer
Carrying email, messaging and video calls between people
questions.explain: A network is two or more computers linked together, and the point of linking them is threefold: sharing resources such as a printer or an internet line, sharing data such as files and databases, and communicating. Encrypting the files sitting on a single machine is a local security measure that a computer can do entirely on its own, with or without a network, so it is not one of the reasons to connect machines together.
why_wrong: One printer or internet line used by everyone on the network is exactly the 'share resources' purpose.
Files and databases accessible from any connected device is exactly the 'share data' purpose.
Email, messaging and video calls are the 'communicate' purpose, and all of them travel over networks.

questions.q: Three of these topology descriptions are correct. Which one is wrong?
options: STAR - all devices connect to one central hub or switch
BUS - all devices share a single central cable
RING - every device connects to one central switch
MESH - devices connect to many or all of the others directly
questions.explain: In a ring, each device connects to exactly two neighbours, so data travels around a loop from one device to the next. Connecting every device to one central hub or switch is the definition of a star, not a ring. Topology simply names the physical or logical layout of the connections, so mixing up the shapes mixes up the topologies.
why_wrong: A star really is defined by every device connecting to one central hub or switch, so this pairing is correct.
A bus really is the layout in which all devices share one single central cable, so this pairing is correct.
A mesh really is the layout in which devices connect to many or all of the others directly, so this pairing is correct.

questions.q: Both a router and a switch are called 'smart' devices, but for different reasons. Which option states what each one is smart at?
options: The router finds the best path between networks; the switch sends data only to the device it is meant for
The router sends data only to the intended device inside one network; the switch finds the best path between networks
Both broadcast data to every connected device, but the router does it faster
The router converts the ISP's signals into a usable form; the switch adds wireless access to a wired network
questions.explain: A router works between networks, for example between your home and the Internet, and its intelligence lies in choosing the best path for traffic. A switch works inside one network and its intelligence lies in delivering data only to the port where the intended device sits. Both are 'smart', but at different jobs and at different scopes.
why_wrong: This swaps the two: path-finding between networks is the router's job, and delivering data only to the intended device inside one network is the switch's.
Broadcasting to every connected device is what a hub does, and it is precisely the behaviour that makes a hub the 'dumb' device of the three.
Converting the ISP's signals is a modem's job and adding wireless access to a wired network is an access point's job; neither describes a router or a switch.

questions.q: Which network device is paired with the correct job?
options: Hub - lets wireless devices join a wired network
NIC - converts signals between your ISP and your network
Modem - converts signals between your ISP and your network
Access point - the hardware inside a device that connects it to a network
questions.explain: The modem is the bridge between your home and your Internet service provider, converting the signals that arrive on the ISP's line into something your network can use and back again. That is why the typical home chain runs Internet to modem to router to your devices. The other three devices in this list each have a different, well-defined job.
why_wrong: Letting wireless devices join a wired network is an access point's job; a hub connects devices within one small old-style network by broadcasting to all of them.
A NIC is the hardware inside a device that connects it to a network; it has nothing to do with the ISP's signals.
An access point is what lets wireless devices join a wired network; the hardware inside the device itself is the NIC.

questions.q: These stages of a web request are listed out of order: (1) your router sends the request out, (2) DNS translates the URL into an IP address, (3) the page data returns to your screen, (4) the request travels across the WAN, (5) the website's server receives it. Which sequence is correct?
questions.explain: After you press Enter, the human-readable name must first be turned into an IP address by DNS, because nothing can be routed to a name. Your own router then pushes that request out of your local network, it crosses the WAN that is the Internet, the website's server receives it, and only then does the page data come back to your screen. The whole round trip usually takes well under a second and crosses PAN, LAN and WAN boundaries on the way.
why_wrong: The router has nowhere to send the request until DNS has turned the name into an IP address, so translation must come first.
The request leaves through your own router before it crosses the wider Internet, not after.
The server cannot receive a request that is still in transit; crossing the WAN comes before the server receives it.

questions.q: Which network type is paired with the correct geographic scale?
options: PAN - a few metres, covering one person's own devices
questions.explain: Networks are classified by how much ground they cover, and the four sizes run smallest to largest as PAN, LAN, MAN, WAN. A personal area network spans only a few metres and ties together the devices one person is carrying, such as earbuds or a smartwatch talking to a phone. Each of the other three names belongs to a bigger scale.
why_wrong: One building or campus is the scale of a LAN; a MAN spans a whole city, such as a cable-TV or traffic-camera network.
Countries and continents is the scale of a WAN, the Internet being the obvious example; a LAN covers one building or campus.
A single city is the scale of a MAN; a WAN reaches across countries or continents.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the six key network devices covered in this unit?
questions.explain: The six key network devices are the router, the switch, the hub, the modem, the access point and the NIC, and each one exists to connect something to something else. A firewall is genuine network equipment in the real world, but its job is filtering or blocking traffic for security rather than connecting devices, and it is not part of this list.
why_wrong: An access point is one of the six: it lets wireless devices join a wired network.
A hub is one of the six: it connects devices within one small network by broadcasting to all of them.
A NIC is one of the six: it is the hardware inside a device that connects that device to a network.

questions.q: Classify these three examples in order: Bluetooth earbuds paired to a phone, a college computer lab, and the Internet itself.
questions.explain: Earbuds and a phone are a couple of metres apart and belong to one person, which is a personal area network. A college computer lab sits inside a single building or campus, which is a local area network. The Internet spans countries and continents, which makes it the textbook wide area network, so the three fall into PAN, LAN and WAN respectively.
why_wrong: A college computer lab is inside one building, which makes it a LAN, not a city-wide MAN.
Earbuds paired to a phone cover a couple of metres of one person's own devices, which is a PAN rather than a building-wide LAN.
The Internet spans countries and continents, so it is the standard example of a WAN, not a city-sized MAN.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the five ways of managing a virtual machine listed in this unit?
questions.explain: The five management actions for a VM are start, stop, snapshot, clone and delete, covering booting it, shutting it down cleanly, saving a state, copying the whole machine and removing it for good. Moving a running VM from one physical host to another is a real feature of virtualization platforms, but it is not one of the five basic actions in this list.
why_wrong: Snapshot is one of the five: it saves the VM's exact state so you can return to it later.
Clone is one of the five: it makes an identical copy of the whole VM.
Delete is one of the five: it permanently removes the VM and frees its resources.

questions.q: Which statement correctly separates a hypervisor from a virtual machine?
options: A virtual machine is the software layer that creates virtual computers; a hypervisor is the software-based computer it produces
A hypervisor is the software that creates and runs virtual machines; a virtual machine is the software-based computer it produces, with its own virtual CPU, memory, disk and OS
They are two names for the same piece of software
A hypervisor is the physical host machine, and a virtual machine is the guest operating system installed on it
questions.explain: The hypervisor is the layer that divides one physical machine so that several independent virtual computers can run on it at once. Each of those virtual computers is a virtual machine, a computer inside a computer, complete with its own virtual CPU, memory, disk and operating system. One hypervisor typically runs several VMs side by side, which is why the two terms cannot be interchanged.
why_wrong: This reverses the two: the hypervisor is the layer doing the creating, not the thing created.
They are distinct layers, and one hypervisor usually runs several virtual machines at the same time on the same hardware.
The physical host is real hardware, not the hypervisor; the hypervisor is software sitting between that hardware, or a host OS, and the guests.

questions.q: What is the difference between taking a snapshot of a VM and cloning it?
options: A snapshot saves the VM's exact state so you can return to it later; a clone makes a separate identical copy of the whole VM
A snapshot makes a separate identical copy of the whole VM; a clone saves its state so you can roll back to it
A snapshot deletes the VM and frees its resources; a clone shuts it down cleanly
Both give you a second running VM, and the only difference is that a clone keeps running while a snapshot is paused
questions.explain: A snapshot is a saved point in time for one machine: the VM carries on, and if something goes wrong you roll it back to that saved state. A clone is a duplicate machine, an identical copy of the whole VM that can be handed to somebody else or run alongside the original. So a snapshot protects one VM against mistakes, while a clone multiplies the VM.
why_wrong: These are swapped: copying the whole VM is cloning, and saving a state you can roll back to is a snapshot.
Removing the VM and freeing its resources is the delete action, and shutting it down cleanly is stop; neither is a snapshot or a clone.
A snapshot does not produce a second machine at all; it is a saved state of the same VM.

questions.q: While creating a virtual machine you create a virtual hard disk and you attach an ISO file. What is the difference between the two?
options: The virtual hard disk is the operating-system installer image, and the ISO is the VM's empty storage
The virtual hard disk is the storage created for the VM, and the ISO is the operating-system install file attached so the VM can install an OS
They are the same file, just named differently by different hypervisors
The virtual hard disk holds the host's files, and the ISO records how much RAM and how many CPU cores were allocated
questions.explain: Creating a VM means opening the hypervisor, choosing a new machine, allocating RAM and CPU cores, creating a virtual hard disk, attaching an OS install file and then booting to install. The virtual hard disk is the blank storage the VM will write to, exactly like an empty drive in a new computer. The ISO is the installation media, the equivalent of the installer disc you boot from to put an operating system onto that empty drive.
why_wrong: This reverses them: the ISO is the operating-system installer and the virtual hard disk is the storage the VM writes to.
They are created at different steps and serve different purposes: you make the empty virtual disk, then attach an OS image to install onto it.
The virtual hard disk belongs to the VM and not to the host, and RAM and CPU cores are allocated in a separate step rather than stored inside an ISO.

questions.q: Which order shows the layers of a virtualised machine correctly, from the bottom upwards?
options: Guest OS, then hypervisor, then the physical host machine
Physical host machine, then guest OS, then hypervisor
Physical host machine, then hypervisor, then guest OS
Hypervisor, then the physical host machine, then guest OS
questions.explain: At the bottom sits the real hardware, the physical host machine. The hypervisor runs on that hardware and carves it up, and each guest operating system, such as Windows, Linux or macOS, runs on top of the hypervisor inside its own VM. Reading the stack this way also explains isolation: the guests never touch each other because the hypervisor stands between them and the hardware.
why_wrong: This is the stack upside down; the guest operating systems sit at the top, not beneath the hardware.
A guest OS cannot sit directly on the physical machine in a virtualised setup, because the hypervisor is what creates and runs it.
The hypervisor cannot sit below the physical machine, since it is software that runs on that hardware, or on a host OS above it.

questions.q: Which VM management action is paired with the correct effect?
options: Stop - permanently removes the VM and frees its resources
Clone - saves the VM's exact state so you can return to it later
Start - boots the VM up from where it left off
Delete - shuts the VM down cleanly so it can be booted again later
questions.explain: Start simply powers the virtual machine on again, picking up from the state it was left in, exactly as switching on a real computer would. The five actions form a neat set: start and stop control power, snapshot and clone preserve or copy the machine, and delete removes it permanently. Mixing the labels is the usual mistake, because stop and delete both end a running VM but only one of them is reversible.
why_wrong: Permanently removing the VM and freeing its resources is delete; stop merely shuts it down cleanly so it can be started again.
Saving the VM's exact state to return to later is a snapshot; a clone produces a whole separate copy of the machine.
Shutting the VM down cleanly so it can boot again is stop; delete removes the machine for good.

questions.q: Three of these statements about Type 2 hypervisors are true. Which one is false?
options: It runs as an application on top of an existing operating system
Oracle VirtualBox and Parallels Desktop are examples of it
It runs directly on the hardware with no host OS, which is why data centres prefer it
It is simpler to set up and is the usual choice for personal virtualization
questions.explain: A Type 2 hypervisor is hosted: it is installed like any other application on top of an operating system you already run, which makes it easy to set up on a personal laptop. Running straight on the hardware with no host OS underneath describes a Type 1 or bare-metal hypervisor, which is the faster arrangement used in data centres. The examples split the same way: VirtualBox, VMware Workstation, VMware Fusion and Parallels Desktop are Type 2, while ESXi, Hyper-V, Citrix Hypervisor and KVM are Type 1.
why_wrong: Running as an application on top of the existing OS is exactly what makes a hypervisor Type 2.
VirtualBox and Parallels Desktop are both listed Type 2 hosted products.
Being simpler to set up and suited to personal virtualization is a genuine Type 2 trait.

questions.q: Which NIST cloud characteristic is paired with the correct meaning?
options: Resource Pooling - the provider's computing resources are pooled and shared to serve many customers
Broad Network Access - the customer pays only for the resources actually consumed
Measured Service - capacity can be added or removed quickly as demand changes
Rapid Elasticity - the customer can obtain resources without any human interaction with the provider
questions.explain: Resource pooling means the provider keeps one large pool of servers, storage and networking and serves many customers out of it, rather than dedicating separate hardware to each. This is what makes a public cloud economical and it is the reason cloud providers run enormous data centres full of hypervisor-managed VMs. The other four traits, self-service, broad network access, elasticity and metering, each describe a different property of a genuinely cloud service.
why_wrong: Paying only for what is consumed is Measured Service; Broad Network Access means the service is reachable over the network from many kinds of devices.
Adding and removing capacity quickly as demand changes is Rapid Elasticity; Measured Service is about metering that usage and billing for it.
Obtaining resources with no human interaction with the provider is On-Demand Self-Service; Rapid Elasticity is about scaling capacity up and down.

questions.q: Which cloud deployment model is paired with the correct example?
options: Private cloud - AWS, Azure and Google Cloud
Public cloud - a single bank's internal cloud
Community cloud - several government agencies sharing one infrastructure
Hybrid cloud - infrastructure open to anyone who signs up
questions.explain: A community cloud is shared by a group of organisations that have needs or rules in common, such as government agencies that must all follow the same regulations, and outsiders cannot rent capacity on it. That places it between a public cloud, which anyone may use, and a private cloud, which belongs to one organisation alone. A hybrid cloud is the fourth model, a connected mix of a private part and a public part.
why_wrong: AWS, Azure and Google Cloud are the standard examples of a public cloud, open to anyone who signs up.
A bank's internal cloud, dedicated to one organisation only, is the standard private-cloud example.
Infrastructure open to anyone is a public cloud; a hybrid cloud connects a private part and a public part, keeping sensitive data private while apps run publicly.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four cloud deployment models?
questions.explain: The four deployment models describe where the infrastructure lives and who is allowed on it: public, private, hybrid and community. 'Distributed' does appear in this unit, but as a type of operating system in which many computers appear to the user as a single system, not as a way of deploying a cloud. Keeping the two lists apart is the point of this question.
why_wrong: Hybrid cloud is one of the four: a connected mix of public and private infrastructure.
Community cloud is one of the four: shared by organisations with needs in common.
Private cloud is one of the four: infrastructure dedicated to a single organisation.

questions.q: Under Platform as a Service, which layers are still the customer's responsibility?
options: The operating system, middleware and runtime
Nothing, because the provider manages every layer
questions.explain: Responsibility shifts from you to the provider as you move from on-premises through IaaS and PaaS to SaaS. Under PaaS the provider takes over storage and networking, servers, virtualization, the operating system, middleware and the runtime, so all you bring is your application code and your data. That is exactly the pizza-delivery idea: the kitchen and the delivery are handled, you only decide what to eat.
why_wrong: The runtime is one of the layers PaaS hands over to the provider, and that handover is precisely what separates PaaS from IaaS.
Operating system, middleware and runtime are all provider-managed under PaaS; they are yours only under IaaS or on-premises.
Having the provider manage every layer, applications and data included, describes SaaS rather than PaaS.

questions.q: Order these four arrangements from the one where the customer manages the most layers to the one where the customer manages the least.
questions.explain: On-premises means you own and manage everything from storage and networking up to the application itself. IaaS hands the provider the storage, networking, servers and virtualization; PaaS additionally hands over the operating system, middleware and runtime; SaaS hands over the whole stack including the application and the data. So responsibility falls away steadily as you move from on-premises to SaaS.
why_wrong: This is the reverse order: SaaS leaves the customer managing the least, not the most.
PaaS and IaaS are the wrong way round, because under IaaS you still manage the operating system, middleware and runtime that PaaS gives to the provider.
On-premises always involves more of your own management than IaaS, since under IaaS the provider already owns the servers, storage, networking and virtualization.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between cloud computing and virtualization?
options: Cloud computing replaced virtualization, so modern providers no longer use hypervisors
Cloud computing is built on virtualization: providers run enormous numbers of hypervisor-managed VMs across their data centres
Virtualization is only possible if you rent the hardware from a cloud provider
They are unrelated, because virtualization is about networks while cloud computing is about operating systems
questions.explain: Cloud computing is renting computing power, storage and software over the Internet, and the way providers actually carve that capacity up for customers is virtualization. Every major cloud data centre runs hypervisors at massive scale, slicing physical servers into the virtual machines that customers rent. That is why virtualization appears one layer down in the service-model table, as something the provider manages from IaaS upwards.
why_wrong: Cloud data centres depend on hypervisors rather than having moved past them; AWS, Azure and Google Cloud all run them at huge scale.
Virtualization works perfectly well on hardware you own, as any student running VirtualBox on a laptop is doing without touching a cloud.
Both are about computing resources: virtualization divides one machine into many, and cloud computing rents such resources out over the Internet.

questions.q: How do Rapid Elasticity and Measured Service differ?
options: Rapid Elasticity means capacity scales up and down quickly with demand, while Measured Service means usage is metered so you pay only for what you use
Rapid Elasticity means usage is metered and billed, while Measured Service means capacity scales quickly with demand
Rapid Elasticity means you can obtain resources yourself without contacting the provider, while Measured Service means resources are shared among many customers
They describe the same idea: the provider pools hardware across many customers
questions.explain: Elasticity is about capacity: the cloud can add servers within minutes when load rises and release them when it falls. Measured service is about accounting: consumption is metered, so the bill reflects only the resources actually used. They travel together in practice, which is why a shop that scales up for a sale and then pays only for those hours illustrates both at once, but they are two separate characteristics.
why_wrong: These are swapped: metering and billing is Measured Service, while scaling capacity quickly is Rapid Elasticity.
Obtaining resources yourself is On-Demand Self-Service and sharing resources among customers is Resource Pooling, so neither half of this option is the pair being asked about.
Pooling hardware across customers is a third, separate characteristic called Resource Pooling; elasticity and metering remain two distinct traits.

questions.q: A five-member class team has four weeks to build a fest website. They split it into the home page, the events page, the registration form and the sponsor page, and four members start working on their own page the same evening instead of waiting for one person to finish. Which benefit of this approach are they getting?
options: Parallel Work — different people can tackle different parts at the same time
Easier Debugging — a mistake is isolated to a specific part, not the whole thing
Reuses Solutions — a solution that worked once is applied to a similar problem
Enables Reuse — the tool keeps working even when its hidden details change
questions.explain: Decomposition splits one big goal into independent parts, and one of its stated benefits is that different people can work on different parts at the same time. Nothing here is being debugged or reused; the entire gain is that four members can work simultaneously because the parts do not depend on one another. This is exactly why software teams break an app into modules before anyone starts writing it.
why_wrong: Easier debugging is also a benefit of decomposition, but it shows up when a mistake has to be traced to one part; no bug is being isolated here.
Reusing a solution on a similar problem is a benefit of pattern recognition, and the four pages are being built separately rather than copied from one another.
Enables Reuse is a benefit of abstraction, where a well-abstracted tool keeps working after its hidden internals change; nothing internal is being hidden here.

questions.q: Ishita has been handed one line of instruction for her semester project: build a system that manages the hostel mess. She has no idea where to begin and has written nothing for three days. Which move should she make first?
options: Write the exact ordered steps the finished program will follow, from start to stop
Break the mess system into smaller sub-problems such as menu, attendance, billing and feedback
Look for similarities between this project and a project a senior did last year
Decide which details of a student record the system can safely ignore
questions.explain: Breaking the problem into smaller parts is almost always the first move, because a problem this large and vague cannot be pattern-matched, simplified or turned into steps while it is still one lump. Once the mess system is split into menu, attendance, billing and feedback, each part is small enough to look for patterns in, strip down and write steps for. The other three moves all become far easier after the split, which is why they come later.
why_wrong: Writing the ordered steps is the algorithm stage, and it only works once you already know what each part has to do.
Pattern recognition comes after the split: you look for patterns in the smaller parts, and at this moment there are no parts yet.
Deciding what to ignore is abstraction, and it is applied to a part of the problem once the parts are known.

questions.q: Ishaan is the only person who uses the TV in his hostel room. He presses volume-up and the sound rises; he has never thought about the infrared code the remote sends or the microprocessor inside the TV that decodes it, and nothing inside the set has changed since he bought it. Which benefit of abstraction is he enjoying?
options: Reduces Complexity — he interacts with a simple model instead of every internal detail
Easier to Share — others can use his solution without needing to understand it fully
Enables Reuse — the tool still works even after its hidden details change
Saves Time — he does not solve the same kind of problem from scratch each time
questions.explain: Abstraction hides everything that does not matter for the task at hand, leaving a simple model — here, one button that means louder. Because Ishaan is the only user and nothing inside the set has changed, the benefit is neither sharing nor reuse: it is simply that he deals with a small control panel instead of infrared codes and decoding circuits. Cutting down what a person must hold in their head is abstraction's first purpose.
why_wrong: Easier to Share is about other people using a solution without understanding it, and the scenario states he is the only person who uses the TV.
Enables Reuse appears when hidden internals change and the simple interface still works; here nothing inside the TV has changed.
Saves Time is a benefit of pattern recognition, and no repeated problem is being solved in this scenario.

questions.q: For a lab exercise Dev writes out his steps for finding the largest number in a list and emails the sheet to two classmates. One works through it by hand on paper; the other has a machine carry the steps out. All three end up with exactly the same answer. Which property of an algorithm does this demonstrate?
options: It is repeatable and shareable — anyone, or any machine, following the same steps gets the same result
It can be expressed many ways — plain English, a flowchart, pseudocode or code
It turns ideas into action — it is the concrete plan that follows decomposition and abstraction
It is finite — it terminates after a limited number of steps
questions.explain: Because every step of an algorithm is clear and follows a definite order, the outcome does not depend on who or what carries it out. That is precisely what the scenario shows: a human working on paper and a machine executing the same written steps produce identical results. This repeatability is what makes an algorithm shareable at all, and it is why steps written by a person can be handed to a computer.
why_wrong: Being expressible in several forms would be the point if the same steps had been written once as a flowchart and once as code; what the scenario highlights is that the results matched.
Turning ideas into action describes an algorithm's place after the earlier building blocks, not the fact that three separate attempts agreed.
Finiteness means the process stops after a limited number of steps; here the issue is that the answers matched, not that the work ended.

questions.q: A biotechnology student plans an experiment by splitting it into stages, noticing that three stages follow the same measuring routine, deciding which variables to ignore, and writing a precise protocol anyone in the lab can follow. Her friend tells her none of this counts as computational thinking because she has not written a single line of code. Who is right, and why?
options: The friend — computational thinking begins only once the solution is written in a programming language
The student — computational thinking is a way of thinking rather than a coding skill, and scientists and designers use it too
The friend — the four building blocks are defined for software problems, so a lab protocol does not qualify
The student — but only because her protocol could later be converted into code
questions.explain: Computational thinking means formulating a problem and expressing its solution so that a human or a machine can carry it out, which says nothing about code. The student has used all four building blocks on a laboratory problem, and scientists, engineers, designers and everyday problem-solvers use exactly the same skills. Writing code is one way to express the result, not a condition for the thinking itself.
why_wrong: The definition explicitly allows a human to carry out the solution, so no programming language is required for the thinking to count.
The same four skills apply to cooking, sports, research and business just as much as to software.
Her protocol is computational thinking in its own right; it does not need a future program to earn the label.

questions.q: A student is asked for the 40th term of the sequence 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 and answers 120 within a second, without writing out any of the terms in between. A classmate insists she must have worked through all forty. What actually let her answer straight away?
options: She spotted the repeating rule, add 3 each time, and applied it directly instead of recalculating from scratch
She broke the sequence into smaller groups of terms and solved each group separately
She ignored the details of the sequence that did not matter and worked with a simplified model
She followed a finite, ordered set of steps that produced the answer as its output
questions.explain: Noticing that every term rises by the same amount replaces a forty-step walk with a single multiplication, which is what pattern recognition buys you: a known rule stands in for repeated work. The same thing happens with 2, 4, 6, 8 — once the rule is visible, any term can be predicted without computing the ones before it. Spotting the repeat is also what lets you reuse an old solution on a familiar-looking problem.
why_wrong: Splitting the sequence into groups would be decomposition, and she would still be adding her way through the terms inside each group.
Ignoring irrelevant detail is abstraction, and a bare numeric sequence has no extra detail to strip away that would produce the 40th term.
Following ordered steps to an output describes an algorithm, and avoiding exactly that walk-through is the point of the scenario.

questions.q: Four teams finish their parts of a food delivery app: user login and profiles, restaurant and menu listings, cart and payment, and order tracking. Each part works perfectly on its own machine, yet there is still no working app for a customer to use. What does the process require next?
options: The separate solutions must be combined into one finished system
Each team must split its own part again until no part can be divided further
The four parts must be rewritten in a single programming language before any of them can run
A pattern must be found among the four parts so that one part can replace the other three
questions.explain: Breaking a problem down is only half the method: the full definition is to split the problem, solve each part, and then combine the solutions. Four flawless modules remain four modules until they are joined into one system that logs a customer in, shows restaurants, takes payment and tracks the order. Skipping the combining step is the most common way a neatly divided project still fails to produce anything usable.
why_wrong: Dividing further serves no purpose once each part is already solved, and it would leave the parts just as unjoined as before.
Nothing in the method requires all parts to share one language; the gap here is integration, not language choice.
Pattern recognition lets a solution be reused across similar parts, but these four do different jobs and none can stand in for the others.

questions.q: A city traffic department has tried fixing jams by intuition for years and the jams keep coming back. A consultant instead maps the junctions one by one, identifies the times of day that repeat, strips away details that do not affect flow, and writes a signal-timing procedure the staff can follow exactly. Which statement best explains why this approach succeeds where intuition failed?
options: Problems like traffic are too big to solve by gut feeling, and this turns a vague, messy problem into clear steps anyone can follow and check
This approach guarantees the mathematically optimal answer to any problem it is applied to
Traffic control is ultimately a programming problem, so only a solution written as code can work
Splitting the city into junctions removes the need for any further analysis of the problem
questions.explain: Computational thinking exists because modern problems such as traffic, epidemics and recommendations are too tangled for gut feeling alone. Its payoff is clarity: a vague problem becomes an ordered procedure that other people can follow and, just as importantly, inspect and check. The consultant's advantage is not a magic answer but a method whose reasoning is visible at every step.
why_wrong: Nothing in computational thinking promises optimality; it promises a clear, ordered, checkable route to a solution.
The same four skills apply to cooking, sports, research and business, and what the consultant delivered is a procedure for human staff, not a program.
Splitting the city is only the first move; the consultant still had to find the repeating patterns, simplify, and write the procedure.

questions.q: On a laptop with a single processor, a student has a browser, a music player, a download manager and a video call all open, and every one of them appears to keep working at the same moment. Which operating system function is directly responsible for that appearance?
options: Process Management — deciding which program gets the CPU, and for how long
Memory Management — allocating and freeing RAM so processes do not collide
Device Management — talking to printers, disks and keyboards through drivers
User Interface — giving the user a GUI or command line to work in
questions.explain: A single processor can execute only one program at any instant, so the sense that four things run together comes from the OS handing the CPU to each of them in turn for a short slice. Deciding who runs next and for how long is process management. The other functions are busy at the same time, but none of them is what shares the processor.
why_wrong: Memory management keeps each program's RAM separate; that matters if one app would overwrite another's data, not for taking turns on the processor.
Device management reaches hardware through drivers, which is not what chooses which of the four programs runs next.
The user interface is what lets the student see and click the four windows, not what divides processor time between them.

questions.q: A video editor and a game are open at once. Neither can read or overwrite the other's working data, and the instant the student quits the game, the space it had been using becomes available to the editor. Which operating system function is at work?
questions.explain: Memory management hands RAM to each running program and reclaims it when the program exits, keeping running processes from colliding in the process. Both clues in the scenario point there: each program's working data is kept apart, and the space returns to the pool the moment the game closes. Deciding when each program runs would be a different function entirely.
why_wrong: Process management decides which program gets the CPU and for how long; it neither hands out nor reclaims RAM.
File management organises stored data into files and folders; the working data described here lives in RAM only while the programs run.
Security and access enforces logins, permissions and isolation between users, and here one user is running both programs.

questions.q: A student saves an assignment, and a week later finds it again by opening a folder named Semester1 and clicking the document's name. She has never known, and never needed to know, which physical part of the disk the bytes actually sit on. Which operating system function gives her this?
questions.explain: File management is the OS job that organises stored data into named files and folders and controls access to them, so people work with names and paths instead of disk locations. Without it the student would have to keep track of where on the platter her assignment lives. Reaching the disk hardware is a separate function that sits underneath this one.
why_wrong: Device management speaks to the disk hardware through drivers; it does not create the folder-and-filename view she is using.
Memory management deals with RAM given to running programs, not with documents that survive between sessions on storage.
Process management schedules programs on the CPU and has nothing to do with locating a saved document.

questions.q: An administrator connects to a rented server that has no monitor, no mouse and no desktop of any kind. All she gets is a blinking prompt where she types commands, and every task she needs is done from there. Which operating system function is she using?
options: User Interface — the OS gives you either a graphical desktop or a command line
None — with no desktop, the user interface function is simply absent on that machine
Device Management — her typing arrives through the keyboard driver
Security and Access — she had to log in before the prompt appeared
questions.explain: The user interface function means giving a human some way to interact with the machine, and a command line is one of the two forms it takes; a graphical desktop is the other. A headless server therefore has a complete user interface, just a textual one. The login check and the keyboard driver are different functions that happen around it.
why_wrong: A command line is a user interface, not the absence of one: the OS still has to accept typed commands and show their results.
The keyboard driver is device management, which explains how keystrokes arrive rather than what gives her a way to work with the system.
Security and access is what verified her login; the prompt she then works at is the user interface.

questions.q: Thirty students are logged in to one university server at the same time, each compiling and running their own programs, and each feels the machine is responding to them personally. There is one set of processors serving all of them. Which type of operating system is this?
questions.explain: A time-sharing OS switches the CPU rapidly between the tasks of many users, so each user gets frequent short turns and the machine feels interactive to everyone at once. That is the classic multi-user UNIX and Linux server model. The identifying clues are many simultaneous interactive users on a single machine, with nobody waiting for a group of jobs to finish.
why_wrong: A batch OS collects jobs and runs them in groups with no direct interaction, the opposite of thirty students working live at their terminals.
A distributed OS makes many computers appear as one system; here one machine is serving many users.
A real-time OS exists to guarantee a response inside a strict deadline, as in a pacemaker or an airbag, not to divide a server among students.

questions.q: A student double-clicks a program icon on a shared lab computer. The disk light flickers, but instead of a window the screen shows a message saying she is not allowed to run this program. Where in the sequence an OS follows when opening an app did it stop?
options: After the program was located, given RAM and scheduled on the CPU, at the permission check — before the interface drew a window
Right at the start, because the OS never found the program file on the disk
During memory allocation, because a program that will be refused is never given RAM
After the window had been drawn, since permissions are only checked once a program is on screen
questions.explain: Opening an app runs through a fixed chain: the OS finds the file on disk, the memory manager allocates RAM, the process manager schedules it on the CPU, the OS checks permissions, and only then does the interface draw the window. A refusal with no window on screen means the chain reached the permission check and went no further. The flicker of the disk light also confirms the file itself was found.
why_wrong: The disk activity and the specific not-allowed message show the file was located; a missing file produces a different failure altogether.
RAM allocation comes before the permission check in the sequence, so memory is given first and the refusal follows.
The window is drawn last, after permissions have already been verified, which is exactly why nothing appeared.

questions.q: At one instant on a laptop, two programs both want the printer, three want more RAM, and all of them want the processor — yet nothing crashes and nothing overwrites anything else. This is why an operating system is compared to an air-traffic controller. What single job do all of the OS's functions radiate from?
options: Managing the machine's resources so competing demands are met without collisions
Translating each program's source code into instructions the processor understands
Providing the applications that the user actually wants to run
Storing the user's documents safely so nothing is lost when the power goes
questions.explain: Every OS function — process, memory, file, device, security and user interface — is one face of a single job: managing resources. Like a controller deciding which plane gets the runway, the OS decides which program gets the CPU, the RAM, the printer and the disk, so nothing collides. Without that arbitration each app would have to address the hardware itself, and multitasking, a shared screen and a file system would all be impossible.
why_wrong: Translating source code is the work of compilers and interpreters, which are tools that run on top of the OS rather than part of its core job.
Applications come from developers; the OS provides the managed environment those applications run inside.
Keeping documents safely stored is part of file management, which is one of the six functions rather than the job all six serve.

questions.q: A college creates an account on one Linux server for each of 300 first-year students, and every account gets its own personal folder for assignments. Under which top-level directory will those 300 folders be found?
questions.explain: /home is the branch of the Linux tree that holds a personal folder for each ordinary user, so a server with 300 accounts has 300 folders sitting there. The administrator is the single exception, with a separate home folder of its own. Everything, including /home itself, still hangs off the one root directory /.
why_wrong: /root is the administrator's own home folder, kept deliberately apart from where ordinary users' folders are created.
/usr holds installed programs and libraries shared across the whole system, not students' personal folders.
/var holds logs, caches and other data that changes as the system runs.

questions.q: An administrator is explaining the Linux tree to a first-year student: settings live in one branch, logs in another, and the everyday commands the student types — ls, cp, mv — are themselves small program files kept in a branch of their own. Which directory holds those everyday command programs?
questions.explain: /bin is the directory set aside for essential user command binaries, which is what ls, cp and mv are. Knowing that these commands are ordinary program files stored in the tree, rather than magic built into the terminal, is part of understanding that everything in Linux lives under one hierarchy. Each other branch has its own distinct purpose in that tree.
why_wrong: /etc holds system-wide configuration files, which are settings rather than runnable commands.
/usr holds installed programs and libraries added to the system, not the essential user command set the student types constantly.
/var holds logs, caches and other variable data that grows and changes while the system runs.

questions.q: A student who has only ever used Windows adds a second hard disk to a Linux machine and asks which drive letter it will get, so he can type something like D: to reach it. What should he be told?
options: Linux has no drive letters: everything lives in one tree starting at the root directory /, and the new disk is reached through a path in that tree
Linux assigns the letter D: to the disk, but only after it has been formatted
Each disk in Linux gets its own root directory, so the new disk will have a second /
Linux can only use one disk at a time, so the second disk has to replace the first
questions.explain: The Linux file system is a single hierarchy: everything, on every disk, hangs off one root directory written as /. Branches such as /bin, /etc, /home, /usr, /var and /root are places within that one tree, and extra storage appears as a path inside it rather than as a separately lettered volume. This is why every absolute Linux path you type begins from /.
why_wrong: Drive letters are a Windows convention; formatting a disk on Linux does not produce one.
A Linux system has exactly one root directory, and a second / would defeat the whole single-tree design.
Linux systems routinely use many disks at once; the extra ones are simply reached through paths within the one tree.

questions.q: Inside a folder called labs, a student has two files: report.txt and data.csv. She wants data.csv gone for good, while the labs folder and report.txt stay exactly as they are. Which command should she type from inside labs?
questions.explain: rm is the command that deletes a file, and naming only data.csv leaves the folder and every other file in it untouched. A different command exists for removing directories, and it is not interchangeable with this one. Being precise about which file you name is what keeps a deletion from taking more than you intended.
why_wrong: rmdir removes an empty directory, so aiming it at a file is simply the wrong tool for the job.
mv moves or renames a file and needs a destination name; on its own it deletes nothing.
cat displays a file's contents in the terminal and changes nothing at all.

questions.q: A student has a file called essay.txt and has decided it should be called final.txt instead. She does not want a second copy lying around afterwards — just one file, under the new name. Which command does exactly that?
questions.explain: mv both moves and renames, so giving it the old name and the new name inside the same folder leaves one file called final.txt and no essay.txt. The real decision here is whether the original should survive: if it should, you copy; if it should not, you move. Only the move satisfies the condition she stated.
why_wrong: cp makes a copy, so she would be left with both essay.txt and final.txt, which is precisely the duplicate she wanted to avoid.
touch would create a new empty file called final.txt and leave her actual essay sitting in essay.txt.
chmod changes a file's permissions and cannot rename anything.

questions.q: A student has written a script called app.py in her project folder. The file is there, and cat app.py prints the code inside it correctly, but the system refuses to run it because the file is not marked as runnable. Which command fixes this?
questions.explain: chmod changes a file's permissions, and +x adds the permission that marks a file as executable so the system will run it. Nothing is wrong with the file's contents or its name here — only with what the file is permitted to do, which is exactly what chmod exists to change. It is the normal step in a Linux project right after the script file is created.
why_wrong: touch creates an empty file or updates an existing one's timestamp; it grants no permission to run anything.
Renaming the file changes what it is called, not what it is allowed to do.
ls only lists the file, and listing something has no effect on whether it can be executed.

questions.q: A student wants to see for herself how her operating system decides which program gets the CPU, and she would like to change part of it and rebuild it to watch what happens. Her friend tells her no operating system lets anyone do that. Which fact about Linux settles the argument?
options: Linux is free and open source, so its actual code can be inspected, modified and learned from
Linux runs over 96% of the world's top 1 million web servers
Linux command-line skills transfer directly to real engineering jobs
Linux is the only operating system that offers a command line
questions.explain: Being free and open source means the source code of the operating system itself is available to read, change and rebuild, which is one of the main reasons Linux is recommended to computer science students. The other true statements about Linux describe where it runs or what skills it builds, not whether you are permitted to open it up. Only the open-source point answers the friend's claim.
why_wrong: The market-share figure explains why Linux matters in industry, but says nothing about being allowed to read or alter its code.
Transferable command-line skills are a genuine reason to learn Linux, yet they concern using the system rather than modifying it.
Many operating systems provide a command line, so this is not a true statement about Linux at all.

questions.q: A research team scatters eight weather sensors across a hilly campus. Each sensor is set up to talk directly to several of the other sensors, with no central box in the middle, so that if one unit dies the readings still reach the base station by another path. Which topology have they built?
questions.explain: In a mesh, devices connect to many or all of the others directly, so between any two points there is usually more than one route. That redundancy is exactly what the team wants: losing one sensor removes some links but not the only path home. The absence of any central device is the strongest clue that this is a mesh rather than a star.
why_wrong: A star needs one central hub or switch that every device connects to, which is precisely what this design leaves out.
A bus has every device sharing one single central cable, so there is one common path rather than many direct device-to-device links.
In a ring each device connects to exactly two neighbours in a loop, so each sensor would have two links, not direct links to several others.

questions.q: An old lab is wired with one long cable running the length of the room, and every computer taps into that same cable. A technician accidentally cuts the cable in the middle and the entire lab drops off the network at once. Which topology is the lab using?
questions.explain: A bus topology is defined by all devices sharing a single central cable, which is exactly how this lab is wired. Because that one cable is the shared path for everybody, damaging it anywhere takes the whole segment down. The decisive detail is the single shared cable that every machine taps into, not the failure itself.
why_wrong: In a star each machine has its own cable to a central hub or switch, so cutting one cable would isolate only that one machine.
A mesh gives devices many direct links to one another, so traffic would simply take another route around a single broken link.
A ring connects each device to exactly two neighbours in a closed loop; there is no single shared cable that everyone taps into.

questions.q: A city corporation joins its water-board office, three zonal offices and the traffic-control room into one network of its own. The offices sit in different neighbourhoods several kilometres apart, but none of them is outside the city. Which type of network is this?
options: LAN, because all the offices belong to one organisation
MAN, because the network spans a single city
WAN, because the offices are several kilometres apart
PAN, because it is a private network of one body
questions.explain: Networks are classified by the geographic area they cover, not by who owns them. A network that stretches across neighbourhoods of one city but stops at the city limits is a metropolitan area network, the same category as a city's cable-TV or traffic-camera network. Anything smaller would sit inside one building or campus, and anything larger would cross cities or countries.
why_wrong: A LAN covers one building or campus; shared ownership does not stretch a LAN across a whole city.
A WAN spans countries or continents, the Internet itself being the classic example; this network stops at the city boundary.
A PAN covers only a few metres around one person and their own devices, such as earbuds paired to a phone.

questions.q: A software company's Bengaluru office and its Toronto office have their networks joined, so an engineer in either city reaches the same file servers as if those servers were down the corridor. Which type of network links the two offices?
options: WAN, since the link spans countries
LAN, since both offices belong to one company
MAN, since each office serves a metropolitan area
PAN, since only the company's own staff use it
questions.explain: Size is what names a network, and a link between two countries falls into the largest category, the wide area network. The Internet itself is the best-known WAN, and corporate links between continents ride on the same scale of infrastructure. Each office may still have its own LAN inside its building; the WAN is what joins them.
why_wrong: A LAN is limited to one building or campus, and company ownership does not change how far a network physically reaches.
A MAN covers a single city, such as a city's cable-TV or traffic-camera network, not two countries.
A PAN is a few metres of range around one person's own devices, like a smartwatch paired to a phone.

questions.q: Ishaan's desktop suddenly cannot reach the network. He unplugs its Ethernet cable, plugs the same cable into his brother's laptop at the same desk and it connects instantly, and every other machine in the flat is online. On his own desktop, no wired network adapter is listed at all any more. Which part has failed?
options: The switch the flat's computers are cabled to
The network interface card inside his desktop
The modem supplied by the ISP
questions.explain: The NIC is the hardware inside a device that actually connects that device to a network, so a device with no working NIC is cut off while everything around it is fine. Every shared part of the chain has been proved healthy: the same cable and port carry another machine online, and the rest of the flat is unaffected. When a fault follows one machine rather than one cable, the failure is inside that machine.
why_wrong: If the switch had failed, the other machines cabled to it would have lost the network too, and the laptop on that same cable would not have connected.
A dead router would stop every device in the flat from reaching other networks, not just this one desktop.
A failed modem would cut the whole flat off from the ISP, yet the rest of the flat is online.

questions.q: A new office has twelve computers cabled to a switch. They share files and a printer with each other perfectly. The ISP's broadband line is live and the modem's lights are normal, yet no computer can open a website. Which device is missing from the setup?
options: A router, to direct traffic between the office network and the Internet
A second switch, so every computer gets a free port
A hub, to broadcast the connection to all twelve machines
An access point, so the computers can connect wirelessly
questions.explain: A switch connects devices within one network, which is why file and printer sharing already works, but it cannot pass traffic between two different networks. Moving data between the office network and the ISP's network is a router's job: it finds the path from one network to the other. The typical chain is Internet, then modem, then router, then the devices, and here the router is the missing link.
why_wrong: Ports are clearly not the problem, since all twelve machines already talk to each other through the existing switch.
A hub only broadcasts inside one small network and is a step down from the switch they already have; it joins no networks together.
An access point lets wireless devices join a wired network; these machines are already cabled and their problem is reaching the Internet.

questions.q: A college lab has thirty computers but exactly one colour printer. Once the lab is networked, a student sitting at any of the thirty machines can send a document to that single printer. Which reason for building a network does this show?
options: Sharing data, since files and databases become reachable from any device
Communication, since email, messaging and video calls travel over networks
Sharing resources, since one printer or Internet line can serve everyone connected
Topology, since the layout decides which devices can reach which
questions.explain: Networks exist to share resources, share data and let people communicate, and here the thing being shared is a piece of hardware. One printer or one Internet line serving every connected machine is the textbook case of resource sharing. The lab did not buy thirty printers because the network lets thirty machines queue at one.
why_wrong: Data sharing is about files and databases being reachable from any machine; nothing in this story is about access to files.
Communication covers person-to-person traffic such as email, messaging and video calls, not access to a shared device.
Topology is the physical or logical layout of the connections, such as star or bus, and is not a reason for networking in the first place.

questions.q: Ananya's browser reports 'server not found' for every site she types by name. When a friend sends her a site's numeric address and she types that instead, the page loads normally. Her modem, router and Wi-Fi all appear to be working. Which step of the journey from URL to web page has broken?
options: The router sending her request out of the home network
The translation of the typed name into an IP address
The website's server receiving the request
The page data travelling back across the WAN to her screen
questions.explain: After a URL is typed, the very next step is DNS translating that name into an IP address, and only then does the request leave the router for the Internet. Reaching sites by their numeric address skips the translation step entirely, so if numbers work and names do not, the name-to-address step is the one failing. Every later step is proved healthy by the pages that do load.
why_wrong: The router is clearly forwarding traffic, because requests made with the numeric address leave the house and return with a page.
The servers are receiving requests perfectly well; the same sites answer when reached by their numeric address.
Return traffic is arriving too, since pages render fully once the numeric address is used.

questions.q: On a Friday night a botched update wrecks a customer's virtual server at a hosting company. Instead of rebuilding the machine and reinstalling everything over the weekend, the operator rolls it back to a saved state and it is serving traffic again ten minutes later. Which reason for using hypervisors does this illustrate?
questions.explain: A crashed or corrupted VM can be restored from a snapshot in minutes instead of the days a physical rebuild would take, and that speed of recovery is one of the main reasons businesses virtualise. The saved state holds the machine exactly as it was, so nothing has to be reinstalled or reconfigured. The damage here was real and already done, and the hypervisor's value was undoing it quickly.
why_wrong: Server consolidation is about replacing many under-used physical servers with one machine running many VMs; no servers were merged in this story.
Safe testing means trying a risky change on a VM before touching the real system, whereas here the bad update already hit the live machine.
Better utilisation is about using a physical server's full capacity instead of leaving it idle, which the ten-minute recovery does not demonstrate.

questions.q: Before applying a major database upgrade to the system the whole college depends on, an administrator installs that same upgrade on a virtual copy of the system first and watches what breaks. Nothing he does inside the copy can touch the live machine. Which reason for using hypervisors is this?
questions.explain: One of the standard business reasons for hypervisors is trying risky updates or unfamiliar software on a VM without touching the real system. The VM is isolated, so a failed upgrade damages only the copy and the production system never sees it. The giveaway is that the risky change is deliberately applied to the virtual system first, before anything real is at stake.
why_wrong: Fast disaster recovery is about restoring a crashed VM from a snapshot in minutes; nothing has crashed here and the live system is untouched.
Server consolidation means turning ten physical servers into one server running ten VMs, a cost and energy argument rather than a testing one.
Broad network access is one of the five NIST traits of cloud services, not a reason for running a hypervisor.

questions.q: Aman's laptop has 16 GB of RAM and one physical SSD. He creates a VM, gives it 4 GB of memory and a 50 GB virtual hard disk, and installs Ubuntu inside it. A friend asks where that VM's memory and disk actually come from. What is the correct answer?
options: The guest OS talks straight to the laptop's hardware and the hypervisor only starts it up
The virtual hard disk is storage the hypervisor vendor supplies over the Internet
The hypervisor carves out a share of the laptop's own CPU, RAM and storage and presents it to Ubuntu as virtual hardware
The VM permanently reserves a separate memory module and disk partition that the host can never use again
questions.explain: A virtual machine is a computer built entirely in software: the hypervisor builds a virtual CPU, memory and disk for it out of the host's real resources. Ubuntu inside the VM sees ordinary hardware and never learns that it is virtual. This is also why deleting a VM frees its resources back to the host.
why_wrong: If the guest reached the hardware directly there would be no isolation between VMs; the hypervisor sits between the guest and the physical machine precisely so one crash cannot take the others down.
A virtual hard disk is just a file on the host's own storage; nothing about it is streamed from a vendor.
Resources are allocated in software and handed back when the VM is stopped or deleted, rather than being carved permanently out of the hardware.

questions.q: Neha opens VirtualBox, clicks New Virtual Machine, gives it 4 GB of RAM and two CPU cores, creates a virtual hard disk and starts the machine. It boots to a black screen reporting that no bootable medium was found. Which step of creating a VM did she skip?
options: Taking a snapshot of the new VM
Attaching an operating-system installation file (ISO) to the VM
questions.explain: Creating a VM runs from opening the hypervisor, through allocating RAM and CPU and making a virtual disk, to attaching an OS install image and booting to install it. A brand-new virtual hard disk is empty, so without an ISO attached the VM has nothing to boot from, exactly like a real PC with a blank drive and no installation media. Attaching the ISO is the step that turns an empty machine into one that can install an operating system.
why_wrong: A snapshot saves the state of a VM that already works; it cannot supply an operating system to a blank machine.
Cloning copies a VM that has already been built, and she is creating hers from scratch, so there is nothing to copy.
Two cores are plenty to reach a boot prompt; the machine is not short of CPU, it simply has nothing to boot.

questions.q: A lab server's disk is nearly full. One VM on it was a one-off experiment that finished last term and nobody will ever open it again, and the team wants its disk space and its assigned resources back permanently. Which VM management action fits?
questions.explain: Deleting a VM permanently removes it and frees the resources it was holding, which is exactly what a team short of disk space needs. The other management actions all assume you still want the machine: start and stop control whether it is running, snapshots preserve a state, and clones duplicate it. Delete is the only one that reclaims space for good.
why_wrong: Stopping shuts the VM down cleanly, but its virtual disk file and its allocation stay on the host, so nothing is freed.
A snapshot saves the VM's exact state so you can return to it later, which adds data to the disk rather than freeing any.
Cloning makes a second identical copy of the whole VM, consuming even more of the space they are short of.

questions.q: A student cannot work out how a cloud provider gives thousands of separate customers each their own private 'server' when every data centre holds a limited number of physical machines. What makes this possible?
options: Each customer is quietly given a slice of time on one shared operating system account
Every customer is allocated one physical machine, which is why providers build such large buildings
The provider's switches split one server's network connection among many customers
Hypervisors run many isolated virtual machines on each physical server
questions.explain: Cloud computing is built on virtualization: providers run enormous numbers of hypervisor-managed VMs across their data centres. One powerful physical server can host many VMs, each with its own guest OS, virtual CPU, memory and disk, and each isolated from its neighbours. That is what lets a finite amount of hardware be rented out as a far larger number of apparently separate servers.
why_wrong: Sharing accounts on one operating system would give no isolation between customers, whereas each VM has its own guest OS and virtual hardware.
One physical machine per customer is exactly the waste virtualization removes, since a single server's full capacity can be used by many VMs.
Splitting a network connection shares bandwidth, not the CPU, memory and operating system that each customer needs.

questions.q: A startup's single rack server runs a Windows system for accounting, an Ubuntu system for the web app and a third Linux system for the database, all at the same time, each behaving like a separate computer with its own operating system. What makes this arrangement possible, and where does it sit?
options: A dual-boot menu, which restarts the server into whichever operating system is needed
A hypervisor, which sits between the physical hardware and the guest operating systems
A switch, which divides the server between the three operating systems
The host operating system's file manager, which keeps each system in its own folder
questions.explain: A hypervisor is software that lets one physical computer run several separate, independent virtual computers at once, and it sits between the physical machine and the guest operating systems it creates. Each guest gets its own virtual CPU, memory and disk and runs simultaneously with the others. Isolation comes from the same arrangement: if one guest crashes, the rest keep running.
why_wrong: A boot menu runs only one operating system at a time and needs a restart to switch, whereas all three systems here run simultaneously.
A switch connects devices within a network and has nothing to do with running several operating systems on one machine.
Keeping files in folders does not give a system its own virtual CPU, memory and disk; that is the hypervisor's job.

questions.q: Rita uploads a photo from her phone on the bus, opens the same photo on her laptop at home that evening, and shows it to her grandmother from a browser on a cyber-cafe machine. She installs nothing special anywhere; each device simply needs an Internet connection. Which NIST cloud characteristic is on display?
questions.explain: Broad network access means the service is reachable over the network from a wide range of ordinary devices, which is why the same photo appears on a phone, a laptop and a borrowed browser. Nothing about the service changes as she moves between them; only the device does. Photo services such as Google Photos are the standard illustration of this trait.
why_wrong: Rapid elasticity is about capacity growing and shrinking with demand, which is not what changes as she moves between devices.
Resource pooling is about many customers sharing the provider's common pool of hardware, which is invisible in this story.
Measured service is about usage being metered and billed, and nothing here is being counted or charged.

questions.q: A provider's data centre serves thousands of customers from one common set of servers and storage. Two rival companies' virtual machines may well sit on the same physical box, and neither customer can say, or needs to care, which machine holds their data. Which NIST characteristic does this describe?
questions.explain: Resource pooling means the provider's compute, storage and network capacity is held in a common pool and served to many customers at once, with the physical location abstracted away. That shared pool is what makes cloud economics work, and it is the reason a customer is given capacity rather than a named machine. Hypervisors are what keep the tenants sharing that hardware isolated from each other.
why_wrong: On-demand self-service is about a customer provisioning a server themselves, in minutes, without a person at the provider approving it.
Broad network access is about reaching the service from many kinds of device over the network, not about how the hardware behind it is shared.
Rapid elasticity is about capacity being added and removed as demand moves; this story is about many customers sharing one pool at the same time.

questions.q: Two students launch their hackathon project with a provider whose sign-up page is open to anybody with a card. Their virtual machine runs in the same shared infrastructure as every other customer in the world, and they pay only for the hours it stays up. Which deployment model are they using?
questions.explain: A public cloud is shared infrastructure open to anyone who signs up, which is exactly what AWS, Azure and Google Cloud offer. The defining feature is who may use it, not how big the customer is: two students and a large corporation rent from the same pool. Nothing here is reserved for one organisation or one closed group.
why_wrong: A private cloud is dedicated to one organisation alone, such as a bank's internal cloud, and is not open to outside sign-ups.
A community cloud is shared by a closed set of organisations with common needs, such as several government agencies, rather than by anyone with a card.
A hybrid cloud joins private and public infrastructure together, and these students have no private infrastructure of their own.

questions.q: A research group needs a very specific Linux version with custom drivers for their simulation code, so they must install and control the operating system themselves. They have no budget to buy, house or cool servers, and want a provider to supply the machines, storage and networking. Which service model fits?
questions.explain: Under IaaS the provider supplies the servers, storage, networking and virtualization, while the customer installs and manages the operating system and everything above it. That split is exactly what this group wants: no hardware to own, but full control of the OS. It is the take-and-bake tier of the pizza analogy, where the base is provided and you finish it yourself.
why_wrong: With SaaS the provider manages everything and you simply use a finished application, so there is no operating system for you to choose.
With PaaS the provider manages the operating system and runtime for you, which is precisely the control this group must keep.
On-premises means buying and running your own hardware, which is the cost they are trying to avoid.

questions.q: A startup keeps the same two cloud servers in place for two months. In April they ran round the clock and the bill was large; in May the team ran them only during office hours and the bill came to roughly half, with an hour-by-hour usage report in the console. Which NIST characteristic is most directly shown?
questions.explain: Measured service means resource use is monitored, reported and charged for, so the bill tracks what was actually consumed. Here the amount of infrastructure never changed; only the hours it ran did, and the metering turned that straight into a smaller invoice. It is the trait behind the idea of paying for cloud the way you pay for electricity.
why_wrong: Rapid elasticity would mean the number or size of the servers grew and shrank with demand, but the same two servers stayed in place throughout.
Resource pooling describes many customers sharing the provider's hardware, which is not what the changing bill reveals.
