On-demand self-service is about creating resources yourself without waiting for anyone's approval, which this billing story does not turn on.

questions.q: A college decides to buy its own servers, house them in a cooled room, install the operating systems itself and hire staff to keep everything running, rather than renting anything from a provider. In the pizza analogy used for the service models, what has the college chosen?
questions.explain: Making pizza at home stands for on-premises computing: you buy the ingredients, own the oven and do every step yourself. The college owns the storage, networking, servers, virtualization, operating systems, middleware, runtime, applications and data, so nothing has been handed to a provider. Each step to the right in the analogy hands another layer over, which is what this college has declined to do.
why_wrong: Take-and-bake is IaaS, where a provider supplies the servers and storage while you install the OS and apps; this college supplies the hardware itself.
Pizza delivery is PaaS, where the provider also manages the operating system and runtime and you add only your code.
Dining at a restaurant is SaaS, where the provider manages everything and you simply use the finished application.

questions.q: A team deploys their web app on a service where they only push code: the provider supplies the servers, the operating system and the language runtime. A security flaw is then found in that runtime, and separately the team's own code is found to be leaking user data. Who is responsible for fixing each problem?
options: The provider patches the runtime; the team fixes its own application code
The team patches the runtime; the provider fixes the application code
The provider is responsible for both, since it supplies the platform
The team is responsible for both, since it chose the platform
questions.explain: On a platform service the provider owns everything from storage and networking up through virtualization, the operating system, middleware and the runtime, while the applications and the data stay with the customer. So a hole in the supplied runtime is the provider's to patch, and a bug in code the team wrote is the team's. Knowing where that line falls is what decides who is accountable after an incident.
why_wrong: This reverses the split: the runtime is part of the platform the provider manages, and nobody but the team can fix the code the team wrote.
The provider manages every layer only under SaaS, where you use a finished application; on a platform you still own the application and its data.
Handing over the operating system and runtime is the whole reason for choosing a platform, so those layers stop being the team's responsibility.

questions.q: For the tech-fest activity Sana writes a numbered page: (1) form the organising team, (2) arrange the budget and sponsors, (3) book the venue and fix the date, (4) plan the events and invite judges, (5) promote the fest and handle registrations. She titles it 'my algorithm for the fest'. What has she actually produced?
options: A decomposition - the list names the smaller sub-problems to be solved, not the ordered steps that solve any one of them
An algorithm - any numbered list written in order counts as an algorithm
Pattern recognition - she spotted that all five items repeat the same routine
An abstraction - she hid the unnecessary details inside each sub-problem
questions.explain: Decomposition breaks a big problem into smaller manageable parts, and that is exactly what her five items are. An algorithm is a finite ordered sequence of clear steps that takes an input and produces an output, but 'arrange the budget and sponsors' is a whole sub-problem, not a step anyone can simply carry out. Each of her five items would still need its own algorithm before anything could actually run.
why_wrong: Numbering alone does not make an algorithm: every step must be unambiguous, directly executable, and lead from an input to a defined output.
Pattern recognition means noticing that separate parts share a routine you can reuse; her five items are five different problems, not one repeated routine.
Abstraction means deciding which details matter and hiding the rest; she has not simplified a system here, she has split a problem into parts.

questions.q: Rahul's study-planner algorithm reads: (1) open the syllabus file; (2) revise the hardest-looking topic for a while; (3) repeat step 2 until you feel confident. Of the five traits of a good algorithm, which one does this description actually satisfy?
options: Input - the syllabus file is a well-defined input, and an algorithm may have zero or more inputs
Definiteness - each step tells the reader exactly what to do
Finiteness - the process is written to come to an end
Output - the plan clearly produces a usable result
questions.explain: The five traits are input, output, definiteness, finiteness and effectiveness, and a flawed algorithm usually breaks several at once rather than just one. Here the syllabus file is a genuine well-defined input, so that trait holds. The rest do not: vague wording destroys definiteness, a loop that ends on a feeling destroys finiteness, and nothing is ever displayed, stored or returned, so there is no output.
why_wrong: 'Hardest-looking', 'for a while' and 'feel confident' can each be read differently by any two people, which is precisely what definiteness forbids.
Step 3 loops until a feeling arrives, so nothing guarantees the process stops after a finite number of steps.
The plan never displays, stores or returns a result, so it has no defined output at all.

questions.q: A team is handed one tangled brief - 'run the whole college fest' - and spends the first day hunting for repeated routines they could reuse. They find nothing useful and get stuck. Their mentor tells them they tried the building blocks in the wrong order. Why does pattern recognition normally come after decomposition?
options: Patterns show up among the smaller parts once the problem has been broken up, so decomposition is almost always the first move
Abstraction must be finished before any other building block can begin
An algorithm has to be written first, because patterns can only be spotted inside finished steps
Pattern recognition only works on numbers and shapes, never on tasks or behaviour
questions.explain: Decomposition is described as the first move in almost every computational-thinking process because most real problems are too big or tangled to attack in one go. Once the fest is split into team-forming, budgeting, venue, events and publicity, the repeated routine - email, follow-up call, written confirmation - becomes visible across the parts. Looking for that routine in the undivided brief gives you nothing to compare.
why_wrong: Abstraction usually follows decomposition and pattern recognition; it is not a mandatory first step for the others.
Algorithms come last: they are the concrete plan you write once you have decomposed, spotted patterns and abstracted.
Patterns are found in shapes, numbers, behaviour and real-world data alike, including everyday tasks such as inviting speakers and judges.

questions.q: Four students split their project into four modules, one each, expecting to work simultaneously. But the design forces module 2 to wait for module 1 to be complete, module 3 to wait for module 2, and so on, so only one person can work at a time. Which specific benefit of decomposition have they lost, while keeping the others?
options: Parallel work - different people tackling different parts at the same time
Easier debugging - a mistake stays isolated inside one part
Manageability - each small part feels far less overwhelming than the whole
Reuse of solutions - a solution that worked once can be applied again
questions.explain: Decomposition is valued for three things: parts that feel manageable, parts that different people can build in parallel, and bugs that stay isolated in one part. Chaining the modules so each waits for the previous one removes only the parallel-work benefit - the work is still split, just no longer simultaneous. Noticing which benefit a design silently costs you is what turns decomposition from a slogan into a planning tool.
why_wrong: Debugging is unaffected: a bug still sits inside a single module, so isolation survives the chaining.
Manageability survives too - each module is still small and much less daunting than the whole project.
Reusing a solution across similar problems is a benefit of pattern recognition, not of decomposition.

questions.q: In 1854 John Snow drew a street map of London showing only cholera cases and water pumps, leaving out shops, house numbers and everything else. Looking at that map, he saw the cases clustered tightly around a single pump. Which building blocks do the simplified map and the clustering represent, in that order?
questions.explain: Drawing a map that carries only cases and pumps is abstraction: keeping the details that matter for the question and hiding every other one. Seeing that those cases repeat around one pump is pattern recognition, which is what turned a mysterious outbreak into a familiar, solvable problem. The famous example is usually quoted for the pattern alone, but the pattern was only visible because the map abstracted the city first.
why_wrong: This reverses the sequence: the simplified map came first, and leaving detail out is abstraction rather than pattern-spotting.
Decomposition would mean splitting the outbreak into separate sub-problems; Snow did not divide the problem, he simplified his view of it.
An algorithm is an ordered sequence of steps producing an output; noticing a cluster on a map is not a step sequence.

questions.q: A monitoring script runs in an endless loop: check whether the server is up, print the result, wait a minute, repeat - forever, until someone kills it. Every step is clear and practical, and it prints results all day. Judged by the five traits of a good algorithm, is it a valid algorithm?
options: No - it never terminates, so it fails finiteness, even though its steps are definite and effective
Yes - it produces output continuously, and output is the trait that matters most
No - it takes no input, and every algorithm must have at least one input
Yes - every step is unambiguous and practically executable, which is all the five traits require
questions.explain: Finiteness demands that an algorithm terminate after a finite number of steps, and a loop deliberately written to run forever cannot meet it. Being definite and effective is not enough, because the five traits must all hold together. Useful software often runs endlessly, but by this course's definition such a process is a program, not a valid algorithm.
why_wrong: Producing output does not excuse an endless process; finiteness is a separate requirement that this script never satisfies.
Zero inputs is explicitly allowed - the traits ask for zero or more well-defined inputs, but at least one output.
Definiteness and effectiveness are only two of the five traits; input, output and finiteness must hold as well.

questions.q: Four teams each build one module of a food-delivery app - login and profiles, restaurant listings, cart and payment, order tracking. Every module works perfectly on its own, but the teams never join them, so there is no working app at the demo. Which part of decomposition did they leave out?
options: Combining the solutions to the parts back into one solution for the whole problem
Breaking the problem into smaller, manageable parts
Spotting the repeated routines shared by the four modules
Hiding each module's internal details behind a simple interface
questions.explain: Decomposition is defined as breaking a complex problem into smaller parts, solving each part, and then combining the solutions. The combining step is the half that gets forgotten, and without it four working modules are still zero working apps. This is why decomposed work needs an integration plan from the start, not just a division of labour.
why_wrong: They did that step well - the app was split into four independent modules, one per team.
That would be pattern recognition, a different building block, and its absence would not by itself leave the app unassembled.
That describes abstraction; missing abstraction would make the modules harder for each other to use, not stop them being joined at all.

questions.q: Building a library app, Zoya decides a book record needs only the title and the author, calling everything else unnecessary detail. Her fine calculator then cannot work, because nothing records the due date. What went wrong?
options: Abstraction hides only the details that do not matter for the problem being solved, and the due date matters for calculating fines
Abstraction means keeping as few fields as possible, so the fine feature should be dropped instead
This is a decomposition failure - the book record should have been split into smaller parts
This is a pattern-recognition failure - issuing and returning a book follow the same routine
questions.explain: Abstraction means focusing on the details that matter for the problem at hand and hiding the rest, which makes it relative to the problem, not an absolute rule about fewer fields. Once fines are part of the problem, the due date is a detail that matters and cannot be abstracted away. Getting the level right is the skill: too much detail overwhelms, too little breaks the solution.
why_wrong: Abstraction is not a race to the fewest fields; it is choosing the right level of detail for the problem being solved.
Decomposition breaks a problem into parts to solve separately; splitting the record into pieces would not bring back a value that was never stored.
Noticing that issuing and returning share a routine would let her reuse code, but it would still leave the due date unrecorded.

questions.q: A game freezes and Priyanka force-quits it. Straight away the 2 GB it was holding becomes available again and her browser speeds up. Which operating-system function is responsible for that memory becoming usable by other programs?
options: Memory management - it allocates RAM to processes and frees it again so processes do not collide
Security and access - it isolates one user's data from another's
Device management - it talks to printers, disks and keyboards through drivers
File management - it organises data into files and folders and controls access
questions.explain: Memory management is the function that allocates RAM to running processes and reclaims it when they end, so nothing collides and nothing stays reserved for a program that is gone. Ending the process is one job; handing its RAM back to everyone else is the memory manager's. Without it, a single crashed program would keep its memory locked away until the machine restarted.
why_wrong: Security enforces logins, permissions and user isolation; here both programs belong to the same logged-in user, so no permission boundary is involved.
Device management drives hardware such as printers, disks and keyboards through drivers, not the working memory of a running program.
File management organises stored data into files and folders on disk, which is separate from the RAM a running program holds.

questions.q: A research group links 40 lab machines so that a simulation can be written and run as though there were one giant computer, with nobody choosing which machine a task lands on. In the next building, a single server lets 40 students log in at once while the CPU switches rapidly between their tasks. Which OS types are these, in order?
questions.explain: A distributed OS makes multiple computers appear to users as a single system, which is exactly what the simulation cluster provides. A time-sharing OS instead takes one machine and switches the CPU rapidly between several users' tasks, which is the shared server. The two are easy to confuse because both serve many people at once - the difference is how many machines are involved and what illusion is being created.
why_wrong: The labels are swapped: many machines presented as one system is distributed, while one CPU shared rapidly among many users is time-sharing.
A batch OS collects jobs and runs them in groups with no direct interaction, but the 40 students are logged in and working live.
A real-time OS exists to guarantee a response within a strict time limit, which nothing in a simulation cluster demands.

questions.q: You double-click an app icon, and six things happen before the app appears. Where does the operating system's permission check sit in that sequence, and which function handles what comes immediately after it?
options: After the process manager has scheduled the program on the CPU, and the user-interface function then draws the window
Before the program file is located on disk, and file management then draws the window
Immediately after RAM is allocated but before CPU scheduling, and device management then draws the window
Only after the window has been drawn, so a program you are not allowed to run can still appear on screen
questions.explain: The round trip runs in order: locate the file on disk, allocate RAM, schedule the program on the CPU, check permissions, then draw the window. The permission check is the last thing the OS settles before you see anything, and the user-interface function does the drawing. Knowing the order matters because each function depends on the previous one having finished its part.
why_wrong: The file must be located before anything else can happen, and drawing windows is the user interface's job, not file management's.
RAM allocation is followed by CPU scheduling, and the permission check comes after that; device management drives hardware, it does not render windows.
The check comes before the window is drawn, which is precisely what stops a program you may not run from appearing.

questions.q: A college server has no monitor, no mouse and no graphical desktop - the administrator works entirely through a text terminal. A classmate concludes that this machine's OS does not have the user-interface function at all. Is he right?
options: No - the user-interface function covers a command line just as much as a graphical one
Yes - the user-interface function means the graphical desktop, so a text-only machine lacks it
Yes - on a server the user-interface function is replaced by device management
No - but only because the administrator's laptop is supplying the interface over the network
questions.explain: The user-interface function is described as giving you a GUI or a command line to interact with everything else, so the graphical desktop is one of two forms it can take. A text terminal is a full user interface, and on servers it is the usual one. Most of the internet runs on machines administered exactly this way.
why_wrong: A graphical desktop is only one form of the interface; the command line is the other, and both count as the same OS function.
Device management drives printers, disks and keyboards through drivers; it never takes over the job of presenting an interface to a person.
The terminal is how the server's own OS presents its interface, so the function belongs to the server regardless of which machine is connecting.

questions.q: A bank collects every cheque scanned during the day and runs them all together as a single overnight job. Nobody sits at a terminal while it runs, and the results simply have to be ready by 6 am. A student argues this needs a real-time OS because there is a deadline. Which classification is right?
options: Batch OS - jobs are collected and run in groups with no interaction, and a 6 am reporting window is not the strict per-event response guarantee an RTOS provides
Real-time OS - any stated deadline, including 6 am, makes a system real-time
Time-sharing OS - the CPU must switch between the thousands of cheques
Distributed OS - the cheques are handled together as one large group
questions.explain: Batch operating systems collect jobs and run them in groups with no direct interaction, which is exactly how early bank cheque processing worked and how this job is described. A real-time OS is defined by guaranteeing a response within a strict time limit for each event, as in airbags and pacemakers, where being late is a failure in itself. A business reporting window is scheduling convenience, not a per-event guarantee, so the word 'deadline' is the trap here.
why_wrong: An RTOS guarantees a response inside a strict time limit for each triggering event; a nightly reporting window is not that kind of guarantee.
Time-sharing exists to switch the CPU between several users' tasks, and here there is a single job with nobody at a terminal.
A distributed OS makes several computers look like a single system to users; grouping work into one job is a different idea entirely.

questions.q: An engineer must choose an operating system for an industrial robot whose arm has to stop within a fixed number of milliseconds every single time a safety sensor fires. Among the OS families covered in this unit, which named system is the right starting point?
questions.explain: A robot arm that must stop inside a hard millisecond limit needs a real-time OS, whose defining promise is a guaranteed response within a strict time limit. VxWorks sits in that family along with FreeRTOS and QNX, and the same family is used for car airbags and pacemakers. The other named systems are perfectly good operating systems, but none of them is built to make that guarantee.
why_wrong: Linux is listed as a time-sharing example, built to switch the CPU between many users' tasks rather than to guarantee a deadline.
z/OS is a batch OS example: it collects jobs and runs them in groups with no direct interaction.
Plan 9 is a distributed OS example, designed to make many machines appear to users as a single system.

questions.q: Which statement about Linux is correct on both of its claims?
options: It is given as an example of a time-sharing OS, and it is the family running most web servers, cloud infrastructure and supercomputers
It is given as an example of a real-time OS, and it is the family running most web servers
It is given as an example of a distributed OS, which is why data centres run on it
It is given as an example of a batch OS, alongside IBM OS/360 and Unisys MCP
questions.explain: Linux appears with UNIX and Multics as a time-sharing OS, the type where the CPU switches rapidly between multiple users' tasks - which is what a multi-user server needs. Separately, it is the OS family behind most web servers, cloud platforms and supercomputers, with over 96% of the world's top million web servers running it. A question like this is only answerable if both the type list and the real-world role are held at once.
why_wrong: The real-time examples are FreeRTOS, VxWorks and QNX; Linux belongs with UNIX and Multics under time-sharing.
The distributed examples are Plan 9, Google Fuchsia and Amoeba; data centres choose Linux because it is free, open and a proven multi-user server OS.
The batch examples are IBM z/OS, IBM OS/360 and Unisys MCP, which run grouped jobs with no direct interaction.

questions.q: A student created a folder called labs and copied report.txt into it. He now wants the folder gone. Using only the commands covered in class, which approach works and why?
options: rm labs/report.txt and then rmdir labs - rmdir deletes only an empty folder, so the file must go first
rmdir labs on its own - rmdir removes a folder together with everything inside it
rm labs on its own - rm deletes folders as readily as it deletes files
mv labs /home/student and then rmdir labs - moving a folder empties it first
questions.explain: rmdir removes a directory but only when that directory is empty, which is the exact condition people forget. rm is the command that deletes a file, so the file inside has to be removed before the folder can go. Chaining the two in the right order is the whole trick here.
why_wrong: rmdir refuses any folder that still has something inside it, which is exactly why this fails while report.txt is there.
rm is introduced as the command for deleting a file; removing the directory itself is rmdir's job.
mv moves or renames a folder, it does not empty it - the file simply travels along inside.

questions.q: A student is told that the binary for a basic command like ls sits in one top-level directory, while a large application she installed later lives with the other installed programs and libraries in a different one. Which pair of directories is that, in that order?
questions.explain: In the single tree that starts at /, essential user command binaries live in /bin, while installed programs and their libraries live under /usr. Both hold executable software, which is why the pair is so easy to swap - the split is between the essentials the system itself needs and the larger software installed on top. Knowing which is which is how you find a program when something goes missing.
why_wrong: The two are reversed: /bin holds the essential user command binaries and /usr holds installed programs and libraries.
/etc holds system-wide configuration files and /var holds logs, caches and other variable data; neither stores program binaries.
/home holds each user's personal folder and /root is the administrator's home folder; they store people's files, not installed software.

questions.q: A terminal session reads: pwd prints /home/student/project; ls prints app.py and notes.txt; the student then runs mkdir old followed by mv notes.txt old/, and finally runs ls again. What does that last ls print?
questions.explain: mv moves a file rather than duplicating it, so after mv notes.txt old/ the file exists only inside old and is gone from the project folder. ls lists everything in the current directory, folders included, so the newly created old appears alongside app.py. If the student had wanted the file in both places, cp rather than mv was the command to use.
why_wrong: mv moves the file instead of copying it, so notes.txt is no longer in the project folder - cp is what would have left both copies.
This misses the new directory: ls lists folders as well as files, and mkdir old created one right here.
app.py was never touched by either command, so it is still listed.

questions.q: pwd prints /home/student/project, and the student wants her shell to be back in /home/student. Using only the commands covered in class, which one does that?
questions.explain: cd is the only command among the five navigation commands that actually changes where the shell is, and giving it a full path from the root moves you straight there. pwd and ls report information, while mkdir and rmdir create and delete folders - none of them relocates the shell. Naming the destination as an absolute path starting at / works from anywhere in the tree.
why_wrong: pwd only prints the folder you are currently in; it is a report, not a move, and it does not act on a path you hand it.
mkdir creates a new folder, and /home/student already exists - creating something would not move her in any case.
rmdir deletes an empty folder; it neither moves the shell nor would it succeed while project still contains files.

questions.q: In an empty project folder a student runs touch notes.txt and then immediately runs cat notes.txt. What appears on screen?
options: Nothing - touch created the file, but it is empty, so cat has no contents to display
An error saying notes.txt does not exist
The name notes.txt, because cat lists the file the way ls does
The file's permissions, because cat reports a new file's access settings
questions.explain: touch creates an empty file, so after it runs the file genuinely exists but holds no text. cat displays a file's contents, and the contents of an empty file are nothing at all - silence here is the correct result, not a failure. The pairing catches people who expect every command to print something.
why_wrong: touch is precisely the command that creates an empty file, so notes.txt does exist by the time cat runs.
Listing the names in a directory is what ls does; cat displays what is written inside a file.
Permissions are what chmod changes; cat has nothing to do with access settings.

questions.q: A service on a Linux server is misbehaving. The administrator must first change a system-wide setting for that service and then read the errors it has been recording. Which two directories does she work in, in that order?
questions.explain: System-wide configuration files live in /etc, so that is where a service's settings are changed. Logs, caches and other data that keeps changing live in /var, so that is where the evidence of what went wrong is read. Fix-then-check is the everyday rhythm of server work, and it moves between exactly these two directories.
why_wrong: The order is reversed: configuration lives in /etc and logs live in /var, so the edit comes first from /etc and the evidence afterwards from /var.
/usr holds installed programs and libraries and /home holds users' personal folders; neither is where a service's settings or logs belong.
/bin holds essential command binaries and /root is the administrator's own home folder, not a store of system configuration or logs.

questions.q: Both mkdir and touch bring something new into existence. Which statement separates them correctly?
options: mkdir is one of the five navigation commands and creates a folder, while touch is a file-management command and creates an empty file
Both are navigation commands; mkdir creates a folder and touch automatically creates a file inside it
mkdir is a file-management command that creates a folder, while touch is a navigation command that moves you into it
mkdir creates a folder and touch renames it, since renaming is what touch is for
questions.explain: The commands split into two groups: the five navigation commands pwd, ls, cd, mkdir and rmdir, and the file-management commands touch, cp, mv, rm, cat and chmod. mkdir belongs to the first group and makes a directory; touch belongs to the second and makes an empty file. Both create, but they create different things and sit in different families.
why_wrong: touch belongs with the file-management commands, and it never creates anything inside a folder by itself.
The groupings are swapped, and touch does not move you anywhere - cd is the command that changes directory.
Renaming a file is done with mv; touch creates an empty file and leaves existing names alone.

questions.q: A college lab is wired so that all 24 PCs have their own cable running to one central box. The college replaces that box, an old hub, with a switch, and leaves every cable exactly where it was. What is the effect?
options: The topology changes from bus to star, and collisions drop because each PC now has its own cable
The topology changes from star to mesh, because a switch creates a direct link between every pair of PCs
The topology is still star; what changes is that data now goes only to the intended PC instead of to all 24, so collisions drop
Nothing changes at all, because a hub and a switch both sit at the centre and connect the same devices
questions.explain: Topology and device intelligence are two separate ideas. The topology is the layout, and all devices connecting to one central hub or switch is a star whichever box sits in the middle, so re-cabling nothing leaves the star a star. What does change is behaviour: a hub is dumb and broadcasts every message to every device, while a switch is smart and sends data only where it is needed, which is what cuts needless traffic and collisions.
why_wrong: The cabling never was a bus: a bus is one shared central cable that every device taps into, and here each PC already had its own cable to the centre before the swap.
Mesh means devices are physically connected directly to many or all of the others; a switch forwarding data intelligently does not create physical links between the PCs.
The layout is unchanged but the device is not, and that difference is the whole point: a hub broadcasts to every port while a switch sends data only where it is needed.

questions.q: Ananya's smartwatch sends her step count to the phone in her pocket over Bluetooth. The phone is connected to her hostel's Wi-Fi, and the fitness app syncs the data onward to the company's server in Germany. Which network types are the smallest and the largest involved, in that order?
questions.explain: Real traffic usually crosses several network sizes on its way, and each hop is classified on its own. The watch-to-phone Bluetooth link is a few metres between one person's own devices, which is a PAN. The hostel Wi-Fi covering the building is a LAN in the middle, and the final hop to a server on another continent is WAN scale, the Internet itself being the standard example.
why_wrong: The hostel Wi-Fi is indeed a LAN, but it is not the smallest link here: the Bluetooth hop from watch to phone is a PAN of a few metres.
A MAN spans a city, such as its cable-TV or traffic-camera network, which is smaller than a link reaching a server on another continent.
Both halves are wrong: the smallest link is the Bluetooth PAN rather than the hostel LAN, and reaching Germany is WAN scale rather than city scale.

questions.q: A startup's 40 desktops are all cabled to two switches. Files fly between desks, the ISP's modem is powered on with a steady line light, but no desktop can open any website. An intern suggests buying a bigger switch. What is actually missing, and why?
options: A bigger switch, because the switch is what shares one internet connection among many devices
A router, because directing traffic between two different networks, the office network and the ISP's, is a router's job and no switch can do it
An access point, because internet traffic has to pass through a wireless link before it can leave a building
A network interface card in each desktop, because the built-in card only handles traffic inside the office
questions.explain: Routers and switches answer different questions. A switch connects devices intelligently within a single network and forwards data only inside it, while a router directs traffic between different networks and finds the best path, which is exactly what is needed between the office network and the ISP's. The usual home or office chain reads Internet, then modem, then router, then the devices, and here the router link in that chain is simply absent.
why_wrong: A switch only connects devices within one network; however large it is, it has no ability to pass traffic to a different network such as the ISP's.
An access point lets wireless devices join a wired network, so it adds Wi-Fi rather than a path out to the Internet.
The desktops already have working network cards, which is precisely why they can exchange files with each other through the switches.

questions.q: After a coaching centre replaces its old hub with a switch, copying files between the lab's own computers becomes dramatically faster, but downloading the same lecture video from the Internet takes exactly as long as it did before. Which explanation is correct?
options: The switch must be faulty, because a working switch speeds up every kind of traffic on a network
The download is being slowed because a switch inspects each frame's destination, and that checking adds delay
Switches speed up downloads only when a hub is still present somewhere to broadcast the incoming data
A switch only improves traffic moving within the local network; the download speed is set by the ISP link, which the swap did not touch
questions.explain: A hub broadcasts every message to every device, so a roomful of machines sharing one hub collide constantly, and replacing it with a switch that sends data only to the intended device removes that local congestion. But the improvement stops at the edge of the local network. Traffic from the Internet still arrives through the modem over the ISP's line, and that line's capacity is unchanged, so a download limited by the ISP stays exactly as fast as before.
why_wrong: A switch is not faulty merely because Internet speed did not change; its job is confined to sending data only where it is needed inside one network.
Sending data only to the intended device is what makes a switch better than a hub, not a source of meaningful delay, and it would not explain why local copying got faster.
A hub only broadcasts to every device and causes collisions, so putting one back would make the local network worse rather than the download faster.

questions.q: An office's access point gives Wi-Fi to every phone and laptop in the building. One five-year-old desktop sitting a metre from that access point shows no wireless networks at all in its settings, not even the neighbours' networks. What is the most likely cause?
options: The desktop has no wireless NIC, the hardware inside a device that actually connects it to a network
The access point has failed, since it is clearly not reaching that corner of the office
The router is refusing the desktop because it has not been given an address yet
The modem cannot handle one more device on the ISP's connection
questions.explain: Seeing no wireless networks at all, not even ones belonging to other people, points at the device rather than at the network. The NIC is the hardware inside a computer that connects it to a network, and an older desktop typically ships with only a wired Ethernet card. With no wireless NIC there is no radio to detect anything, so the fix is to add one or to run a cable from the desktop to a switch.
why_wrong: Every phone and laptop in the building, including ones much further away, are connected through that same access point, so it is working.
A device that is refused an address still sees the network name listed; this desktop detects no wireless networks whatsoever, which is a hardware-level absence.
The modem's job is converting signals between the ISP and the network, which has nothing to do with whether a desktop can detect a Wi-Fi signal at all.

questions.q: Everyone else in the hostel opens a particular news site normally. On Ananya's laptop the site's name fails every time, yet typing that site's raw IP address into the same browser loads the page instantly. Which part of the journey is broken on her machine?
options: The router, which is failing to send her requests out of the hostel network
The website's server, which is not receiving her requests
The step that translates the site's name into an IP address
Her laptop's NIC, which cannot reach the network at all
questions.explain: The journey from a typed address to a visible page runs in a fixed order: you enter the address, the name is translated into an IP address, the router sends the request out, it crosses the WAN, the server receives it, and the page data comes back. Bypassing the name by typing the IP address directly proves every later step is working. That isolates the fault to the single step she skipped, which is name-to-IP translation.
why_wrong: If the router were not sending her requests out, the raw IP address would fail as well, but it loads instantly.
The server is plainly receiving and answering her requests, since the page arrives whenever she uses the IP address.
A dead network card would leave her with no connectivity at all, not with a working connection that fails only on names.

questions.q: A factory is laying out a control network for 12 machines. The requirement is that each unit be wired directly to many of the others, so that more than one path exists between any two units and nothing depends on a single central box or a single shared cable. Cost is not a concern. Which topology fits?
questions.explain: Mesh is the layout in which devices connect directly to many or all of the others. That density costs a great deal of cabling, which is why it is chosen only where redundancy matters more than money, and it is the one arrangement with neither a central device nor a shared cable that everything relies on. The requirement here describes those properties almost word for word.
why_wrong: In a star every device connects to one central hub or switch, which is exactly the single central box the requirement rules out.
In a ring each device connects to exactly two neighbours, so no unit is directly linked to many of the others as the requirement demands.
In a bus every device shares one single central cable, which is the shared line the requirement explicitly forbids.

questions.q: Vikram's college has six buildings spread across one campus, all linked by cabling that the college itself owns and maintains. A classmate insists this must be a MAN because it spans more than one building. Which classification is correct?
options: MAN, because a MAN is defined by covering more than one building
WAN, because several buildings means several separate networks joined together
PAN, because the network belongs to a single organisation rather than to the public
LAN, because a LAN covers one building or campus, while a MAN spans a whole city
questions.explain: Network types are named by geographic scale, not by how many buildings are involved or who owns the cable. A LAN covers one building or one campus, and a college campus network is the textbook case of exactly that. The next size up, a MAN, spans a city, like a city's cable-TV or traffic-camera network, and a WAN stretches across countries or continents.
why_wrong: Building count is not the dividing line; the scale is what matters, and a MAN spans a city such as its cable-TV or traffic-camera network.
A WAN reaches across countries or continents, the Internet being the standard example, which is far beyond a single campus.
A PAN covers a few metres around one person, such as earbuds paired to a phone; ownership plays no part in the classification.

questions.q: Rohit took a snapshot of his Ubuntu VM before an experiment, finished with the course, and then deleted the VM in VirtualBox to free disk space. A month later he wants that saved state back. What is his position?
options: He can restore it, because snapshots are stored independently of the virtual machine they belong to
The state is gone: deleting a VM permanently removes it and frees its resources, and a snapshot is only a saved state of a machine that no longer exists
He can recover it by creating a new empty VM with the same name, which will pick the snapshot back up
The hypervisor keeps deleted machines automatically, so restarting it rebuilds the VM
questions.explain: The VM management actions are not interchangeable, and delete is the one with no undo, since it permanently removes the machine and releases its resources. A snapshot saves a particular VM's exact state so that you can return to it later, which only means something while that VM still exists. To keep a prepared environment safe from deletion you need a clone, an identical copy of the whole VM kept somewhere else.
why_wrong: A snapshot is a saved state of one particular virtual machine to return to later, not a standalone backup that outlives the machine.
Giving a new machine the same name creates a different, empty VM; it does not recover storage that has already been freed.
Delete is defined as permanently removing the VM and freeing its resources, so nothing is quietly kept behind for a restart to find.

questions.q: Priya runs four VMs on one server. When the Windows VM's operating system crashes during an update, the other three carry on without a hiccup. Two weeks later the server's power supply dies and all four VMs go down together. Which statement explains both events correctly?
options: Isolation protects each VM from the others' software failures, but every VM still depends on the one physical machine they all share
The hypervisor's isolation failed during the power event and should have kept the other three running
VMs are isolated from one another only when each is given its own physical disk
A Type 1 hypervisor isolates crashes, whereas a Type 2 hypervisor would have kept the VMs running through the power failure
questions.explain: Safe isolation means that if one virtual machine crashes the others keep running, because the hypervisor keeps each VM's software world separate from its neighbours. That guarantee is about software faults, not about the hardware underneath. Every VM is still built on one physical host, so anything that takes out the host, whether power, a dead disk or someone switching it off, takes every VM with it.
why_wrong: Isolation means one VM's crash does not spread to its neighbours; no hypervisor can keep software running on hardware that has lost power.
Isolation comes from the hypervisor keeping each virtual machine separate, not from handing each one a separate physical disk.
A Type 2 hypervisor sits on a host operating system on that same dead hardware, so it would fare worse rather than better.

questions.q: On a laptop with 8 GB of RAM, Karan creates three VMs and allocates 4 GB to each. Running any single one of them is fine, but the moment all three are started together the laptop and every VM crawl. What explains this?
options: Type 2 hypervisors are limited to 4 GB of RAM in total, so the extra allocations are ignored
The slowdown comes from the virtual hard disks, since memory allocation has no effect on a VM's speed
The VMs' virtual memory is carved out of the host's single 8 GB of physical memory, so promising 12 GB in total does not create memory the machine does not have
Starting several VMs at once breaks their isolation, so they begin competing for each other's memory
questions.explain: A virtual machine's CPU, memory and disk are software constructs, but they are served by the host's real hardware. A hypervisor can divide the host's 8 GB among several VMs and will often let you promise more than exists, yet the physical total never grows. Three machines each allocated 4 GB on an 8 GB laptop leaves the host and its guests fighting over memory that was never there.
why_wrong: No such fixed cap exists; what actually limits the VMs is how much physical RAM and CPU the host machine has.
Allocating RAM and CPU cores is one of the defining steps of creating a VM precisely because those allocations govern how it performs.
Isolation means one VM's crash does not affect the others; it was never a promise of unlimited resources, and it does not break under load.

questions.q: A hospital's IT team follows two rules. Every risky update is applied first to a duplicate VM that nobody depends on, and a saved state of each production VM is kept so that a crashed machine is back in minutes rather than days. Which two reasons for using hypervisors are these, in that order?
options: Fast Disaster Recovery, then Server Consolidation
Safe Testing, then Fast Disaster Recovery
questions.explain: Trying a risky update on a duplicate machine first is Safe Testing, since you can break the copy without touching the real system. Keeping a saved state so a crashed VM is restored in minutes is Fast Disaster Recovery, which is what makes taking snapshots worth the trouble. Both flow from the same underlying fact: a VM is software, so it can be duplicated and rewound in ways a physical server cannot.
why_wrong: Server consolidation means replacing many physical servers with VMs on one machine to save cost and energy, and no servers are being consolidated in either rule.
Better utilisation is about using a server's full capacity and safe isolation is about one VM's crash not affecting others; neither describes testing updates or restoring a crashed machine.
The order is reversed and consolidation does not appear at all: the first rule is about testing safely, the second about recovering quickly.

questions.q: Arjun opens VirtualBox, clicks New Virtual Machine, allocates 4 GB of RAM and two cores, creates a 40 GB virtual hard disk and clicks Start. The VM window opens and reports that no bootable medium was found. Which step did he skip?
options: Attaching an OS install file (ISO), so the VM has something to boot from and install
Taking a snapshot of the VM before its first boot
Cloning the VM so that the copy is able to boot
Allocating more CPU cores, since a VM cannot start an operating system on two
questions.explain: Creating a VM follows a fixed sequence: open the hypervisor, create the machine, allocate RAM and CPU, create a virtual hard disk, attach an OS install image, then boot and install. The virtual disk Arjun made is empty, because it is the blank drive rather than the operating system. With no ISO attached there is no installation media, so the machine has nothing to start from, exactly as a real PC with a blank disk and no install media would report.
why_wrong: A snapshot saves an existing state to return to later, and there is no state worth saving on a machine that has never booted.
A clone is an identical copy of the whole VM, so cloning an empty machine simply produces a second empty machine.
Two cores are ample, and in any case a shortage of cores would make a VM slow rather than leave it with nothing to boot.

questions.q: An intern runs a small internal service inside a VM on VirtualBox on her office Windows desktop. It works well, except that the service disappears for ten minutes every time Windows installs updates and restarts. Which change fixes the cause, and why?
options: Take a snapshot of the VM before each Windows update so the service can be restored afterwards
Clone the VM onto a second Windows desktop so that one copy is always available
Move the VM onto a server running a Type 1 bare-metal hypervisor, which runs directly on the hardware with no host operating system underneath it to reboot
Allocate more RAM and CPU cores to the VM so that it keeps running while Windows restarts
questions.explain: A Type 2 hypervisor is an application running on top of an existing operating system, which makes it simple to set up but ties every VM's uptime to that host OS. When Windows reboots, the hypervisor and all its guests go down with it. A Type 1 bare-metal hypervisor such as VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V or KVM runs straight on the hardware with no host OS in the way, which is why data centres run services on Type 1.
why_wrong: A snapshot preserves state, but the service would still be offline for every reboot, and the outage rather than data loss is the problem.
A second copy on another Windows machine inherits the same weakness, because that host reboots for its own updates.
No amount of allocated RAM or CPU lets a guest keep running when the operating system hosting the hypervisor shuts down.

questions.q: A teacher must hand each of 30 students an identical, fully configured lab VM, and during the session each student must be able to undo their own mistakes and put their machine back exactly as it started. Which pair of VM actions does this call for?
options: Take one snapshot of the master VM per student, and have each student clone their machine before starting
Clone the master VM once per student, and have each student take a snapshot before starting the exercise
Clone the master VM once per student, and have students clone again whenever they want to undo a mistake
Give all 30 students the one master VM and rely on delete and recreate whenever someone makes a mistake
questions.explain: Clone and snapshot solve two different problems. A clone is an identical copy of the whole VM, which is how you give thirty people the same prepared environment on their own machines. A snapshot saves one VM's exact state so it can be returned to later, which is how a student undoes an afternoon of mistakes in seconds. Used together they provide distribution and a safety net.
why_wrong: Snapshots are states belonging to one machine rather than a way to hand out thirty machines, and a student cloning their own VM does not restore its original state.
Cloning repeatedly makes extra full copies and eats disk and memory, while returning one machine to an earlier state is exactly what a snapshot exists for.
One VM cannot serve thirty students at once, and delete permanently removes a machine along with everything configured on it.

questions.q: A provider runs the VMs of many unrelated customers on the same physical servers, shifting memory and CPU between them as demand moves, and no customer knows or chooses which machine their VM sits on. Which NIST characteristic does this most directly describe?
questions.explain: Resource pooling is the trait in which a provider's computing resources serve many customers from one shared pool, reassigned as demand moves, with the customer generally unaware of the exact physical location. It is what makes the other traits affordable, since a pool used by many customers can be sliced for each of them on demand. Hypervisors are the technology that makes this safe, because each customer receives an isolated virtual machine.
why_wrong: Rapid elasticity is about capacity growing and shrinking quickly with demand; here a fixed pool is simply being shared out among customers.
Measured service is about usage being monitored and billed for what is actually consumed, which this description never mentions.
Broad network access is about reaching the service from any device over the network, not about how the provider's hardware is shared.

questions.q: A student opens the same cloud storage account from her phone on mobile data during a bus ride, from her laptop on the hostel Wi-Fi that night, and from a lab PC's browser the next morning, with no special software installed on any of them. Which NIST characteristic is this?
questions.explain: Broad network access means the service is available over the network through ordinary, standard means and can be reached from whatever device is at hand, from a phone to a lab desktop. The point is that the account rather than the device holds the state, so nothing has to be installed or carried around. That is why the same files appear everywhere she signs in.
why_wrong: On-demand self-service is about provisioning resources yourself, instantly, without waiting for a person at the provider, and nothing is being provisioned here.
Rapid elasticity is about capacity scaling up and down with load, which is unrelated to how many devices she signs in from.
Resource pooling describes the provider serving many customers from shared hardware, which is invisible in this story.

questions.q: A hosting company bills its customers to the exact gigabyte-hour of storage used. However, adding capacity means emailing its support desk and waiting about a day for a technician to make the change. Which reading of the NIST characteristics is correct?
options: All three of metering, elasticity and self-service are satisfied, since the customer does end up with the capacity requested
Rapid elasticity is satisfied but measured service is not, because per-hour billing is too fine-grained to count as metering
Measured service is satisfied, but rapid elasticity and on-demand self-service are not
None of the five characteristics is satisfied, because pay-per-use billing is not one of them
questions.explain: The five NIST traits are tested one at a time, and a service can meet some while missing others. Metering usage and charging only for what was consumed is measured service, which this company does very precisely. Rapid elasticity means capacity appears and disappears quickly as demand moves, and on-demand self-service means the customer provisions it themselves without human interaction at the provider, so a support ticket and a day's wait fails both of those.
why_wrong: A day's wait for a technician is the opposite of provisioning capacity yourself in minutes as demand changes.
Billing to the gigabyte-hour is exactly what measured service means, namely usage that is monitored, controlled and reported.
Measured service is one of the five traits and this company meets it precisely; what it lacks is speed and self-service, not metering.

questions.q: A startup deploys on Google App Engine, so the provider runs the servers, the operating system and the runtime. A bug in the startup's own code corrupts several customer records, and nobody had arranged backups. Who was responsible for the application and the data?
options: The provider, because PaaS means the provider manages everything above the bare hardware
The startup, because under PaaS the application and the data stay with the customer while the provider takes over from the runtime downwards
The provider for the data and the startup for the code, since stored data is part of the platform
Neither, because responsibility for application data applies only to on-premises systems
questions.explain: Moving from on-premises to IaaS to PaaS to SaaS hands more and more layers of the stack to the provider. PaaS takes the runtime, middleware, operating system, virtualization, servers, storage and networking off the customer's plate, which is exactly why you can push code without configuring a server. Applications and data are the two layers the customer still owns on PaaS, and only SaaS moves those to the provider as well.
why_wrong: PaaS gives the provider the runtime, middleware, OS, virtualization, servers, storage and networking, but not the applications or the data running on top of them.
Data is a customer responsibility in every model except SaaS; a platform hosting a database does not make the provider the owner of what the customer puts into it.
Responsibility for data never disappears, it only shifts along the stack, and on PaaS it has not shifted to the provider.

questions.q: A bank builds cloud infrastructure in its own data centre, used by the bank alone and shared with no other company. On top of it, it offers internal teams a service where developers push code and it simply runs, with no server, operating system or runtime for them to configure. How should this be classified?
options: Private cloud as the deployment model, PaaS as the service model
Private cloud as the deployment model, IaaS as the service model
Hybrid cloud as the deployment model, PaaS as the service model
Public cloud as the deployment model, SaaS as the service model
questions.explain: Deployment model and service model answer two independent questions. Deployment asks where the infrastructure lives and who may use it, and infrastructure dedicated to one organisation is a private cloud. Service model asks how much of the stack the provider runs, and managing the servers, operating system and runtime so the customer supplies only code is PaaS. A private cloud can perfectly well offer IaaS, PaaS or SaaS internally.
why_wrong: Under IaaS the developers would be handed servers and storage and would still have to install and manage the operating system, which is exactly what they are being spared.
Hybrid means private and public infrastructure connected together, and nothing in this arrangement runs on public infrastructure.
Public cloud is shared infrastructure open to anyone, and SaaS would mean handing developers a finished application rather than a place to run their own code.

questions.q: A firm runs its application on AWS and keeps its backups on Azure. It owns no servers of its own and rents no dedicated infrastructure anywhere. In a meeting someone calls this a hybrid cloud. Is that right?
options: Yes, because combining two clouds of any kind is what hybrid means
No, it is a community cloud, because two providers are sharing the firm's workload
Yes, because the backups are effectively private, as only the firm can read them
No, this is public cloud on two providers; hybrid means public and private infrastructure connected together
questions.explain: Deployment models describe who the infrastructure belongs to and who is allowed to use it. Public cloud is shared infrastructure open to anyone, which is what both AWS and Azure are, so renting from two of them is still public cloud. Hybrid specifically means a mix of public and private connected so they work together, the classic shape being sensitive data kept on private infrastructure while applications run on public.
why_wrong: Hybrid is defined by mixing deployment models rather than by counting vendors, and both AWS and Azure are public cloud.
A community cloud is infrastructure shared by several organisations with common requirements, such as government agencies, not two vendors serving one customer.
Private cloud means infrastructure dedicated to a single organisation; data being confidential on shared public infrastructure does not make that infrastructure private.

questions.q: One physical machine in a provider's data centre serves several unrelated customers at once. Each has full administrator rights over their own operating system and none can see the others' files. A student asks what makes this possible, and who is responsible for that layer under IaaS.
options: A Type 2 hypervisor runs on the provider's host operating system, and under IaaS the customer manages that virtualization layer
A Type 1 hypervisor splits the machine into isolated VMs, and under IaaS the virtualization layer is the provider's responsibility
There is no hypervisor: the operating system's file permissions keep the customers apart, and the customer manages the OS
The network switches divide the machine between customers, and the provider manages that division
questions.explain: Cloud computing is built on virtualization, with providers running enormous numbers of hypervisor-managed VMs so that a single physical server can safely host many customers, each inside an isolated virtual machine with its own operating system. Data centres use Type 1 bare-metal hypervisors because they run directly on the hardware with no host OS in between and are faster. In the IaaS responsibility split the provider owns storage and networking, servers and virtualization, while the customer's share starts at the operating system.
why_wrong: Data centres run Type 1 bare-metal hypervisors for speed, and virtualization is a provider-managed layer under IaaS, with the customer's responsibility starting at the operating system.
File permissions separate users inside one operating system; they cannot give several customers an administrator-level operating system each on the same machine.
Switches connect devices within a network, whereas dividing one server into several independent machines is the hypervisor's job.
